article_content: Tinder, the popular dating app, is now connecting roughly five million users every single day—while its users swipe through a staggering 750 million profiles in the same timeframe. According to founder and CEO Sean Rad, this explosive growth stems from how closely the app mirrors natural human interactions—but improves upon them. At the Upfront Summit in Los Angeles, Rad explained that in everyday life, we unconsciously signal interest through body language and context. Tinder, he said, simply makes those subtle cues visible and actionable. He emphasized that the most successful profiles aren’t stiff headshots, but images that reveal personality: someone hiking, laughing with friends, or skiing. 'People want to see who you really are,' Rad noted. He also encouraged users to mention shared interests or mutual connections, something you’d never get to know instantly in a real-life encounter. Since launching 18 months prior, Tinder has facilitated close to one billion matches. Daily engagement is high too: users open the app an average of seven times a day. A major boost came during the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics, when athletes in the Olympic Village turned to Tinder en masse, causing a 400% spike in daily usage overnight. Rad admitted the platform is undeniably image-driven—but isn’t apologetic about it. 'It’s all about the picture,' he said. 'And if your photo looks like a passport photo, you’re probably not getting swiped right.'

article_content: Joe Bennett scored his first goal for Aston Villa as they sealed a 1-0 victory over Houston Dynamo, concluding their pre-season tour of Texas on a high note. The decisive moment came just four minutes before halftime, when the left-back rose to head home a precise cross from Andreas Weimann. Having defeated FC Dallas 2-0 earlier in the week, Villa returned to Birmingham with a perfect record from their Texas trip—and with a trophy in hand. The friendly was officially dubbed 'The Charities Cup,' adding a charitable touch to their campaign. Despite a slow start, Villa grew into the match. Fabian Delph forced a save after a dynamic run, while Karim El Ahmadi rattled the crossbar with a curling 25-yard strike. Delph exited due to a minor knock, replaced by Kieran Richardson. After the break, Villa continued to press. Darren Bent missed two clear chances, and Alan Hutton headed a free-kick straight at the keeper. Gary Gardner came agonizingly close to sealing the win in stoppage time, striking the post. Houston’s best opportunity came late, when Brian Ownby skewed a good chance wide. Villa’s defense held firm under pressure from substitutes, maintaining their clean sheet. Manager Paul Lambert expressed satisfaction with his squad’s resilience in the sweltering Texas heat. 'It was hard to play in these conditions—but I was delighted with them again,' he said. 'Another win, and it rounds off this mini-tour perfectly.' Villa’s next friendly is against Chesterfield on Wednesday, followed by matches against Groningen, Walsall, and Parma.

article_content: Michael Zehaf-Bibeau, the 32-year-old gunman who attacked the Canadian Parliament and killed soldier Cpl. Nathan Cirillo last week, exhibited a profile familiar to many lone-actor attackers: alienation from mainstream society, unstable employment, transient living patterns, a history of petty crime, and substance abuse. His subsequent conversion to or reconnection with Islam, coupled with a jihadist mindset shaped by online propaganda from groups like ISIS, reflects a recurring pattern among such individuals. Whether these actors should be classified as 'lone-wolf terrorists' or mentally disturbed criminals remains debated. As the FBI notes, 'There is no single, universally accepted definition of terrorism.' For many, radicalization offers not theological depth, but a sense of purpose, identity, or rebellion. Most lack a nuanced understanding of Salafism—the conservative Islamic ideology underpinning groups like al-Qaeda—and their writings are often incoherent. Many perceive radical Islam as redemption for past failures and a justification for hostility toward authority and society, which they blame as 'kuffar'—nonbelievers—for their corruption. Analysis of dozens of cases reveals that while many had troubled childhoods, there is no evidence they disproportionately come from impoverished backgrounds. Often, they drift into drugs and low-level crime in their late teens or early twenties, sever ties with family, and become radicalized either through radical preachers or online content. Zehaf-Bibeau had multiple run-ins with law enforcement and was charged at least twice with drug-related offenses. Those who knew him described him as erratic and constantly moving; his family said they had not seen him in five years. He communicated with Hasibullah Yusufzai, a militant Islamist in Vancouver, via social media, though Yusufzai relocated to Syria earlier this year, making the extent of his influence uncertain. Similar patterns emerged in other cases: Zale Thompson, a 32-year-old former U.S. Navy member involuntarily discharged over drug issues, attacked four NYPD officers with a hatchet and was shot dead. He had been arrested six times and converted to Islam two years prior. Richard Reid, the 'shoe bomber' of 2001, was similarly troubled—impulsive, involved in minor crime, and detained in a youth facility before embracing Islam under radical imams in London. Muktar Said Ibrahim, leader of the 2005 London bombings, migrated to the UK from Eritrea at age 14, struggled in school, committed muggings, and was radicalized during incarceration alongside Reid. Mohammed Ali Baryalei, born a Muslim, arrived in Australia from Afghanistan as a child. He endured abuse, battled depression, worked as a nightclub bouncer in Sydney’s red-light district, and abused substances until a spiritual awakening in 2009. His path to militancy was swift; he is now believed to be an ISIS leader attempting to incite attacks in Australia. Abdel-Majad Abdel Bary, a London DJ and rapper, expressed in his lyrics a desire for redemption from drug use through faith. He also cited his father’s arrest on terrorism charges as a traumatic catalyst. Like Baryalei, he joined ISIS and publicly shared images of himself holding a severed head of a Western hostage. Identifying such individuals remains difficult, as they typically operate without organizational ties. Can we detect those drifting toward violence before they act? Governments face a dilemma: invest in surveillance and harsher laws, or prioritize prevention and community-based outreach? Programs like the UK’s 'Channel' initiative—which offers counseling, education, job training, and rehab—have received over 4,000 referrals since 2007. Canada uses real-life narratives to spark dialogue in communities. Yet, Public Safety Canada admits: 'Family members, peers, religious leaders, teachers, and social workers are vital in recognizing subtle signs of radicalization.' Still, early intervention does not guarantee prevention. Criminologist Andrew Silke argues that those most likely to engage with such programs are often not the ones authorities fear most. Debate persists: should efforts focus on changing beliefs (de-radicalization) or merely preventing violence (disengagement)? Zehaf-Bibeau reportedly became enraged when Canada and Libya denied him a passport. Yet, after being charged with robbery, he once begged a court to imprison him for a year to overcome his crack cocaine addiction. A psychiatrist deemed him fit for trial, but he received only a one-day sentence. His addiction, anxiety, and extreme religiosity formed a dangerous mix—but the only official response was passport denial. As governments struggle with limited resources and public resistance to outreach programs, many are turning increasingly toward surveillance and punitive policies. Australia is debating laws allowing secret searches and extended preventive detention. The UK has largely dismantled its community-focused Prevent program, opting instead for passport seizures and mandatory de-radicalization orders. James Brandon of the International Centre for the Study of Radicalisation argues this shift represents 'an admission of a grave defeat': rather than stopping radicalization, states are now merely trying to catch perpetrators before they strike. With lone actors remaining elusive and resources stretched thin, the challenge of detection is unlikely to diminish.

Muktar Said Ibrahim, líder de los atentados de Londres de 2005, emigró al Reino Unido desde Eritrea a los 14 años, tuvo dificultades en la escuela, cometió atracos y se radicalizó durante su encarcelamiento junto a Reid. Mohammed Ali Baryalei, nacido musulmán, llegó a Australia desde Afganistán siendo niño. Sufrió abusos, luchó contra la depresión, trabajó como portero en clubes nocturnos del distrito rojo de Sídney y consumió sustancias hasta una revelación espiritual en 2009. Su camino hacia el militancia fue rápido; se cree que ahora es un líder del EI intentando incitar ataques en Australia. Abdel-Majad Abdel Bary, un DJ y rapero de Londres, expresó en sus letras el deseo de redención del uso de drogas a través de la fe. También citó el arresto de su padre por cargos de terrorismo como un catalizador traumático. Al igual que Baryalei, se unió al EI y compartió públicamente imágenes de sí mismo sosteniendo la cabeza decapitada de un rehén occidental. Identificar a estos individuos sigue siendo difícil, ya que normalmente operan sin vínculos organizacionales. ¿Podemos detectar a quienes se desvían hacia la violencia antes de que actúen? Los gobiernos enfrentan un dilema: invertir en vigilancia y leyes más duras, o priorizar la prevención y el enfoque comunitario. Programas como la iniciativa británica 'Channel' —que ofrece consejería, educación, capacitación laboral y rehabilitación— han recibido más de 4.000 referencias desde 2007. Canadá utiliza relatos reales para generar diálogos en comunidades. Sin embargo, Seguridad Pública Canadá admite: 'Los miembros de la familia, pares, líderes religiosos, maestros y trabajadores sociales son vitales para reconocer señales sutiles de radicalización.' Aún así, la intervención temprana no garantiza la prevención. El criminólogo Andrew Silke argumenta que quienes más probablemente participen en tales programas no son los que las autoridades más temen. Persiste el debate: ¿deberían los esfuerzos centrarse en cambiar creencias (desradicalización) o simplemente evitar la violencia (desvinculación)? Zehaf-Bibeau supuestamente se enfureció cuando Canadá y Libia le negaron un pasaporte. Sin embargo, tras ser acusado de robo, una vez rogó a un tribunal que lo encerrara por un año para superar su adicción a la cocaína en piedra. Un psiquiatra lo declaró apto para juicio, pero recibió solo un día de prisión. Su adicción, ansiedad y extrema religiosidad formaron una combinación peligrosa —pero la única respuesta oficial fue la negación del pasaporte. Mientras los gobiernos luchan con recursos limitados y resistencia pública a los programas de outreach, muchos recurren cada vez más a políticas de vigilancia y sanciones punitivas. Australia debate leyes que permiten registros secretos y detención preventiva prolongada. El Reino Unido ha desmantelado en gran medida su programa Prevent centrado en la comunidad, optando por incautar pasaportes y exigir programas obligatorios de desradicalización. James Brandon del Centro Internacional de Estudio de la Radicalización argumenta que este cambio representa 'una admisión de una grave derrota': en lugar de detener la radicalización, los estados ahora simplemente intentan capturar a los perpetradores antes de que actúen. Con actores solitarios siguiendo siendo elusivos y los recursos escasos, el desafío de la detección es poco probable que disminuya.

article_content: By Liz Hull. Scroll down for video. The widow of a man who died after waiting nearly an hour for an ambulance said yesterday that she was 'disgusted' after learning that leaders at the trust responsible for the delays had won an award for 'excellence.' Joyce Pring, 63, said she was 'astounded' to see photographs of staff from the Welsh Ambulance Service Trust (WAST) celebrating at a taxpayer-funded prize ceremony. The award — granted despite repeated failures to meet patient response targets — came just months after the inquest into the death of her husband of 38 years, Fred. Fred Pring died at his home near Mold. In heartbreaking testimony, the inquest heard how Mrs. Pring, a retired civil servant, made four increasingly desperate 999 calls pleading for help, eventually telling operators: 'It’s too late now, he’s gone.' It later emerged that at the time of her calls, six of the 16 ambulances serving her area were on mandatory rest breaks, eight were queued outside hospitals awaiting patient handovers, and the remaining two were responding to other emergencies. After the inquest, Coroner John Gittins criticized WAST’s practices and urged the trust to address risks posed by mandatory breaks and prolonged A&E delays. Yet within weeks, WAST applied for the GateHouse Award for Excellence in Organisational Development. Despite consistently missing the government’s target — that ambulances must reach at least 65% of Category A calls within eight minutes — the trust won the award from the Healthcare People Management Association. Staff attended a ceremony in London earlier this month to collect the honor. Photos from the event show employees dancing and celebrating. Mrs. Pring, of Mynydd Isa, near Mold, North Wales, said she was 'astounded' by the award. 'It is unbelievable that a trust which, month after month, fails to achieve its targets is being rewarded for incompetence,' she said. 'People are dying because of this. The public doesn't realize they're spending time applying for awards while their performance is so dire — to win this beggars belief.' 'What really grates is that they were preparing their application during the inquest. It’s horrifying. I wouldn’t mind if they’d waited until after implementing changes, but doing this while the inquest was ongoing is an insult.' WAST has met the government target in only one month over the past two years. In May 2014, only 54.1% of Category A calls in Wales were responded to within eight minutes — down from 62.5% the previous year. In response to Mrs. Pring’s complaint, a WAST spokesperson said: 'We acknowledge our emergency response times have been consistently below target and recognize we must change this urgently. We are working diligently to improve our clinical practice. Where our staff have contributed to progress, we want to celebrate, recognize, and express pride in our workforce.'

article_content: Following a successful meeting between Tony Abbott and Barack Obama at the White House yesterday, the Australian Prime Minister retracted his previous negative remarks about the U.S. president, describing Mr. Obama as 'charismatic' and 'inspirational'. Mr. Abbott, who is currently in the U.S. meeting with senior leaders, had previously characterized Mr. Obama as leading one of the most left-wing administrations in the past 50 years. 'Look, it was a bit of ill-judged commentary—I hope I've grown beyond that,' he said. During their one-hour meeting, Abbott denied any personal or political conflict between them, adding, 'This is a person who didn’t become president easily. He got there because he possesses considerable leadership ability.' President Obama returned the compliment, stating that Australia is one of the United States' closest allies and a valued military partner. 'Aussies know how to fight,' Obama said. 'I like having them in a foxhole if we're in trouble.' 'There are only a handful of countries in the world we can always count on—not just because they share our values, but because they have real capacity. Australia is one of those countries. We share foundational beliefs in liberal democracy, human rights, and a world order governed by international law and norms. I can't think of a better partner.' The remarks come as the U.S. considers renewed military intervention in Iraq amid escalating violence, including insurgent advances near Baghdad. The leaders also discussed defense strategy, China, and climate change—an area of disagreement—and reaffirmed their commitment to the Trans-Pacific Partnership. The meeting was attended by U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry, Vice President Joe Biden, Australian Ambassador Kim Beazley, and Abbott’s chief of staff, Peta Credlin. President Obama indicated openness to deploying additional troops, saying, 'What we’ve seen over the last couple of days underscores how much more help Iraq will need.' Abbott assured Obama that Australia remains an utterly dependable ally: 'The United States has borne heavy burdens to secure freedom and prosperity for many nations—not just itself. It should never have to carry that load alone.' Obama commended Abbott for increasing Australia’s defense spending during difficult economic times. As a symbolic gesture, Abbott presented Obama with a nine-foot custom-built surfboard adorned with the U.S. Presidential Seal and the flags of both nations, along with a pair of R.M. Williams boots.

article_content: Samsung has approached BlackBerry about acquiring the company for up to $7.5 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by Reuters. The Korean tech giant aims to gain access to BlackBerry’s extensive patent portfolio. The proposed deal could lead to the discontinuation or integration of BlackBerry’s underperforming handsets into Samsung’s Galaxy lineup. Samsung initially proposed a price range of $13.35 to $15.49 per share — a premium of 38% to 60% over BlackBerry’s current trading price. Executives from both companies, advised by financial intermediaries, met last week to discuss the potential transaction. The discussions remain confidential, and sources requested anonymity. Following the news, BlackBerry shares surged as much as 30% on heavy trading volume in New York. The offer implies an enterprise value of $6 billion to $7.5 billion, assuming conversion of $1.25 billion in convertible debt. In November, BlackBerry and Samsung announced a high-profile security partnership, integrating BlackBerry’s security platform with Samsung’s software for Galaxy devices. Neither company has commented further on the acquisition rumors. Last month, BlackBerry launched the BlackBerry Classic, a device centered on a physical 35-key backlit keyboard, long battery life, and enterprise-grade security — features favored by loyal business users. The phone retails for $449 in the U.S. and CAD $499 in Canada, available via Amazon.com and BlackBerry.com, with wider carrier distribution planned through AT&T and Verizon. BlackBerry once commanded nearly 50% of the U.S. smartphone market in 2009 but now holds a small fraction, having been overtaken by Apple and Android devices. The company has struggled to modernize its operating system quickly enough to compete. CEO John Chen, who took office 13 months ago, is steering BlackBerry toward becoming an enterprise software and security provider. While the Classic targets die-hard fans — including public figures like Kim Kardashian and former President Barack Obama — Chen has stated he has no interest in hiring celebrities, saying, 'It's not a waste of money, but a question of where you should spend it today.' To reduce manufacturing costs, BlackBerry partners with Foxconn — the same company that produces Apple’s iPhones — to design and assemble its devices, including the Classic. Foxconn also manages inventory, easing operational burdens on BlackBerry. Chen aims to sell 10 million phones annually, though analysts like Colin Gillis of BGC argue the Classic will remain a niche product. 'The future of this company is not the hardware,' Gillis noted. BlackBerry continues expanding its mobile security software offerings for non-BlackBerry devices to offset declining hardware sales.

article_content: Richard Mannington Bowes, 68, lies in critical condition after being violently assaulted while attempting to extinguish a fire set by rioters outside a supermarket in Ealing, West London, on the evening of August 8, 2011. He suffered severe head injuries and remains in a coma on life support. His identity was confirmed only after neighbors recognized his description and police used his keys to enter his home. Detective Chief Inspector John McFarlane of Scotland Yard said the attack may escalate to a murder investigation. He appealed for anyone with information—especially surveillance footage—to come forward. Eyewitness Peter Firstbrook, 60, described how he and three other bystanders dragged Bowes away from the flames as rioters surrounded them. 'His leg was nearly in the fire,' Firstbrook told the Telegraph. 'I couldn’t move him alone, so I asked for help—three young men stepped in, helped carry him to an alley, then vanished.' Firstbrook noted Bowes showed no external injuries but was bleeding from the ear, suggesting internal trauma. Police have released CCTV images of a suspect: a Black man in his early twenties, wearing a white T-shirt with text and a dark-colored jumper. He is believed to have participated in looting before the attack. Officers arriving at the scene around 10:45 p.m. were overwhelmed by dozens of rioters hurling bottles and bricks. Riot squads eventually pushed back the mob to allow paramedics to reach Bowes. Bowes, originally from Bournemouth, reportedly lived alone and kept to himself. His phone and wallet were stolen during the assault. Residents, including 31-year-old Tom Wakeley, joined efforts to douse burning wheelie bins with fire extinguishers and water after the attack. McFarlane urged the suspect to surrender: 'Do the decent thing and give yourself up.' He also appealed to the public: 'Your mobile footage could be crucial in bringing those responsible to justice.'

article_content: One of the young Libyan rebels credited with capturing Muammar Gaddafi in a drainage ditch nearly a year ago has died from injuries sustained after being kidnapped, beaten, and slashed by supporters of the late dictator. The death of Omran Shaaban — hospitalized in France — has heightened fears of escalating violence and reprisals in northern Africa. The newly elected National Congress has authorized police and the military to use force if necessary to apprehend those who abducted Shaaban and three companions in July near Bani Walid. Shaaban, 22, was hailed as a 'dutiful martyr' by the National Congress. However, his family says he never received the promised reward of one million Libyan dinars ($800,000) for helping capture Gaddafi on October 20, 2011, in Sirte, where the former leader was later killed by revolutionary fighters. His body was returned to his hometown of Misrata, where over 10,000 people gathered to pay their respects at a funeral held at the city’s stadium. Photos showed a wooden coffin with a glass panel revealing Shaaban’s face, his head covered in white gauze. Shaaban and his friends were ambushed while driving home from a vacation near el-Shimekh, close to Bani Walid — a town still dominated by Gaddafi loyalists. Despite being armed, Shaaban was shot twice and paralyzed from the waist down. He and his companions were detained by local militiamen. President Mohammed el-Megarif visited Bani Walid this month and secured the release of Shaaban and two others; a fourth remains captive. When Shaaban finally arrived home, his brother Abdullah described him as 'skin and bones,' severely weakened, barely conscious, and bearing deep razor wounds across his chest. 'His face had changed. It wasn’t my brother that I knew,' Abdullah said. Shaaban was later flown to France for advanced medical care but succumbed to his injuries. He was a member of Libya Shield, a major militia coalition backed by the Defense Ministry. Bani Walid remains a defiant enclave: residents display portraits of Gaddafi at weddings, play his speeches on car stereos, reject the national anthem, and resist the revised school curriculum. The town is heavily armed with weapons leftover from the civil war. In Misrata, anger has mounted. Residents blame Bani Walid fighters for atrocities committed during the conflict, and now demand justice for Shaaban. His eldest brother, Walid, vowed: 'I plan to pursue his rights legally — and join if there is a military incursion. We are going to death, God willing.' A family friend added: 'If the government does not go in, we are going in. Our patience has limits.' Despite promises of punishment, the Libyan government continues to struggle to disarm militias and assert control over territories like Bani Walid — a challenge made more urgent by recent violence, including the September 2012 attack on the U.S. Consulate in Benghazi that killed four Americans, including the ambassador.

article_content: If seeing GIFs across the web isn’t enough to satisfy your craving for short moving clips, you can now buy a machine that plays them without electricity or an internet connection. Called the Giphoscope, this custom-built device transforms GIFs, short video clips, and Vine animations into a sequence of printed images on flip pages. Users crank a handle on the side to turn the pages, creating the illusion of motion—much like a flip book. The Giphoscope is inspired by the 19th-century Mutoscope, an early motion picture device invented by Herman Casler in 1894. Like flip books, it displayed sequential images on flexible cards rotating around a central wheel. Traditionally mounted at eye level for standing viewers, the Giphoscope is a modern, desktop reinterpretation. Each Giphoscope is handcrafted in Italy and costs €300 (£251), plus shipping. Images are printed on paper and mounted on an aluminum core attached to a wooden base, secured with adhesive pads. The crank operates via ball bearings for smooth rotation. After customers submit a digital GIF, designers customize the metal finish, handle, and base color to match the artwork. Production takes seven to ten days per unit. Separately, Brooklyn-based designers Sha Hwang and Rachel Binx founded Gifpop!, a company that prints animated GIFs onto lenticular film—a material known for its prismatic, depth-like effect that animates as the viewer shifts perspective. This technology, dating back to the early 20th century, became popular in children’s stickers and notebooks during the mid-1900s. Hwang and Binx launched a Kickstarter campaign for Gifpop! that was fully funded within hours. Beyond custom orders, they plan to release limited-edition runs featuring work by GIF artists Mr Div, 89-A, and Davidope.

article_content: NEW DELHI: Polar bear numbers in Greenland have declined over the past 20,000 years, according to an international study analyzing their genetic material, diet, habitat, and historical climate data. Researchers, including scientists from the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, attribute this decline to rising sea temperatures, which reduce sea ice and, in turn, limit access to seals—the polar bear’s primary food source. 'When sea temperatures rise, sea ice diminishes, leading to fewer seals for polar bears to hunt,' said Michael Westbury, assistant professor at the University of Copenhagen and lead author of the study published in Science Advances. 'Even small increases in water temperature and minor reductions in sea ice can cause a dramatic drop in polar bear populations. The relationship is not linear.' The study found that sea temperatures around Greenland rose by 0.2 to 0.5 degrees Celsius over the last 20,000 years, correlating with a 20 to 40 percent decline in polar bear numbers. Researchers link this warming to long-term global warming, which is especially evident in Greenland and the wider Arctic. 'The current rate of change is unprecedented compared to anything polar bears have experienced in the last 20,000 years. With projected warming, we may see the species unable to survive,' Westbury warned. Eline Lorenzen, a professor at the University of Copenhagen and co-author of the study, added: 'We’re facing potential sea temperature increases of 2 to 5 degrees Celsius around Greenland—ten times greater than the warming seen over the past 20 millennia. The outlook for polar bears is grim.' 'As apex predators, polar bears reflect broader changes in Arctic marine ecosystems,' Lorenzen noted. 'Their struggle signals deep ecological stress.' The study also revealed dietary adaptability in polar bears. In East Greenland, males and females have developed distinct feeding patterns to avoid competition: males consume multiple seal species, while females primarily target ringed seals. 'This behavioral flexibility shows how some species can adjust when resources become scarce,' Westbury said.

'Cuando aumentan las temperaturas del mar, el hielo marino disminuye, lo que lleva a menos focas para que los osos polares cazan,' dijo Michael Westbury, profesor asistente de la Universidad de Copenhague y autor principal del estudio publicado en Science Advances. 'Incluso pequeños aumentos en la temperatura del agua y leves reducciones en el hielo marino pueden causar una caída drástica en la población de osos polares. La relación no es lineal.' 'Su lucha señala un profundo estrés ecológico.' El estudio también reveló flexibilidad dietética en los osos polares. 'Esta flexibilidad conductual muestra cómo algunas especies pueden adaptarse cuando los recursos escasean,' dijo Westbury.

article_content: On October 29, 2012, Shirley Wort, 63, visited her father Ron Spiller’s grave at Easthill Cemetery in Frome, Somerset, to lay flowers ahead of the 20th anniversary of his death. She was horrified to find the grave buried under four feet of soil and clay, with only the top of the tombstone visible. Workers from Mendip District Council, operating a JCB excavator, were preparing adjacent graves and had displaced soil onto her father’s plot. The cemetery’s standard procedure involves placing excavated earth beside graves — but when surrounding plots are occupied, soil can temporarily cover neighboring graves. Wort, a retired receptionist and co-founder of the charity Cardiac Risk in the Young (CRY) following the 2000 death of her son Julian, criticized the council for its lack of care. 'I was gobsmacked and angry,' she said. 'They had no respect for the dead or their families. All they had to do was place the soil behind the grave.' Her 85-year-old mother was equally distressed upon hearing the news. Wort also noted previous complaints about the neglected condition of her son Julian’s grave. In response, a Mendip District Council spokesperson apologized, stating: 'We deeply regret that Mrs. Wort found her father’s grave in this condition. Our contractor follows standard practice, but we acknowledge this can be upsetting. In this instance, the soil was removed from her father’s grave while she was present.'

article_content: The Hague, Netherlands — The war crimes trial of former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic was abruptly suspended on Thursday, just one day after it began, due to the prosecution’s failure to disclose all evidence to the defense, according to court spokeswoman Nerma Jelacic. Prosecutors had planned to present evidence linking Mladic to the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which approximately 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed. However, the defense requested a halt after discovering that key materials had not been shared, violating procedural rights under tribunal rules. It remains unclear what specific evidence was withheld or how long the delay will last—possibly several weeks. Legal teams are scheduled to meet with the judge later Thursday to determine next steps. The prosecution admitted to an oversight that emerged as they presented their opening case on Wednesday. Mladic, 70, is charged with 11 counts of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity for his role in the 1992–1995 Bosnian War. During the trial’s opening, Mladic exhibited defiant behavior, including making a throat-cutting gesture toward victims in the gallery and refusing to enter a formal plea. He has also claimed poor health and repeatedly sought delays. Prosecutor Dermot Groome detailed how ethnic cleansing was not incidental but a deliberate strategy under Mladic’s command. Testimonies included harrowing accounts of sexual violence, such as a woman raped over 50 times and others forced to commit sexual acts against family members. The trial, held at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), is expected to last years. Among those present were families of Srebrenica victims, many of whom have waited nearly 20 years for justice. Human Rights Watch’s Param-Preet Singh stated, 'His trial should lay to rest the notion that those accused of atrocity crimes can run out the clock on justice.' Mladic evaded capture for 16 years until his arrest in May 2011 in northern Serbia, where he was found hiding in a utility room. He surrendered peacefully despite carrying two handguns. His extradition to The Hague followed shortly after. The trial follows other landmark rulings, including the conviction of former Liberian President Charles Taylor in April 2012, underscoring a global shift toward holding even the most powerful accountable for atrocities.

La fiscalía planeaba presentar pruebas que vinculan a Mladic con la masacre de Srebrenica en 1995, en la que murieron aproximadamente 8.000 hombres y niños musulmanes. Sin embargo, la defensa pidió una pausa tras descubrir que materiales clave no habían sido compartidos, lo cual viola los derechos procesales establecidos por el tribunal. Aún no se sabe qué evidencia específica se omitió ni cuánto durará el retraso —posiblemente varias semanas. Los equipos legales se reunirán con el juez más tarde este jueves para decidir los siguientes pasos. La fiscalía reconoció un error que surgió al presentar su caso inicial el miércoles. Mladic, de 70 años, enfrenta 11 cargos de genocidio, crímenes de guerra y crímenes contra la humanidad por su papel en la guerra de Bosnia entre 1992 y 1995. Durante la apertura del juicio, Mladic mostró conducta desafiante: hizo un gesto de cortarse la garganta hacia las víctimas en la sala y se negó a ingresar un plea formal. También ha alegado problemas de salud y ha solicitado múltiples aplazamientos. El fiscal Dermot Groome explicó que la limpieza étnica no fue un efecto secundario, sino una estrategia deliberada bajo el mando de Mladic. Los testimonios incluyeron relatos impactantes de violencia sexual, como el de una mujer violada más de 50 veces y otras obligadas a realizar actos sexuales contra familiares. El juicio, que se lleva a cabo en el Tribunal Penal Internacional para la ex-Yugoslavia (TPIY), se espera que dure años. Entre los asistentes estaban familias de las víctimas de Srebrenica, muchas de las cuales han esperado casi dos décadas por justicia. Param-Preet Singh, de Human Rights Watch, dijo: 'Su juicio debe poner fin a la idea de que quienes son acusados de crímenes atroces pueden retrasar la justicia hasta que se les agote el tiempo.' Mladic evadió la justicia durante 16 años hasta su arresto en mayo de 2011 en el norte de Serbia, donde fue hallado oculto en una habitación de servicio. Se rindió sin resistencia a pesar de llevar dos armas de fuego. Su extradición a La Haya se realizó poco después. Este juicio sigue otros hitos judiciales, como la condena del ex presidente liberiano Charles Taylor en abril de 2012, lo que refuerza la tendencia global de responsabilizar a los más poderosos por crímenes atroces.

article_content: In 2013, Tahira Bano, a 37-year-old woman from Rochdale, was convicted of severe animal neglect after abandoning a starving puppy on a roadside. The small Staffordshire Bull Terrier, believed to be only six to eight weeks old, was found wrapped in a blanket, weighing a dangerously low 18.7 pounds — less than half the healthy weight for her breed. She was severely dehydrated and suffering from hypothermia, and veterinarians had no choice but to euthanize her just hours after rescue. Bano initially told police she had simply found the dog, but after public appeals and investigations by the RSPCA, she was identified as the owner. Authorities revealed the RSPCA had already visited her home three times between 2011 and 2012 following neighbor complaints about poor dog care. At Bury Magistrates Court, she was found guilty and sentenced to 18 weeks in jail — suspended for two years — along with 100 hours of community service and a £2,000 fine. She was also barred from owning any dog for 15 years. Despite overwhelming evidence, Bano maintained her innocence, claiming the puppy wasn’t hers. The presiding magistrate noted her refusal to take responsibility made mitigation nearly impossible. Her defense highlighted that she had no prior criminal record. RSPCA Inspector Jason Bowles condemned her denial as deeply unethical, stressing how vital public trust is in reporting animal abuse. The case remains a stark reminder of the consequences of ignoring animal welfare — even when the law offers second chances.

article_content: At least 120 people are feared dead and 270 others injured after gunmen and suicide bombers attacked the Grand Mosque in Kano, northern Nigeria, during Friday prayers this afternoon. Witnesses reported three separate explosions and said armed assailants opened fire on worshippers at the mosque in Kano, Nigeria’s second-largest city. Nigerian Captain Ikechukwu Eze confirmed the blasts occurred as hundreds gathered for Friday sermons led by the city’s chief imam, with prayers underway at 2 p.m. local time. A crowd surveyed the wreckage left by the bombings. A damaged vehicle stood amid the destruction. The Emir of Kano, the second-highest Islamic authority in Nigeria, had called last week for citizens to arm themselves against the Islamist militant group Boko Haram — widely believed to be behind the attack. One eyewitness told the BBC’s Focus on Africa: 'The imam was about to begin prayers when he saw a man in a car trying to force his way into the mosque. When people blocked him, he detonated the device. Everyone began running in panic.' Reports differ on whether the Emir was present during the attack. Smoke rose from the mosque as hundreds fled the scene. The attack followed a foiled bombing at a mosque in Maiduguri earlier today — five days after two female suicide bombers killed over 45 people in that city. National police spokesman Emmanuel Ojukwu told AFP that the bombers detonated their devices in quick succession, then gunmen opened fire on those trying to escape. Remains of victims were rushed to Murtala Mohammed Specialist Hospital for burial according to Muslim rites. Ojukwu could not confirm whether the bombers were male or female, noting a recent rise in attacks by women. He also did not provide an exact number of gunmen but said an angry mob killed four attackers in the chaos. Boko Haram, responsible for the April kidnapping of more than 200 schoolgirls from Chibok, has waged a guerrilla campaign since 2009 to establish a hardline Islamic state in northern Nigeria. More than 1.5 million Nigerians displaced by the group have flooded refugee camps across the northeast, where overcrowding and shortages of food, water, and medical care persist.

Una multitud observaba los restos destruidos tras los bombardeos. Un vehículo dañado yacía entre los escombros. El Emir de Kano, la segunda autoridad islámica más alta de Nigeria, había pedido la semana pasada a los ciudadanos que se armaran contra el grupo militante islamista Boko Haram — ampliamente considerado responsable del ataque. El portavoz nacional de policía Emmanuel Ojukwu dijo a la AFP que los terroristas detonaron sus artefactos en rápida sucesión, y luego los hombres armados dispararon contra quienes intentaban escapar. article_content: On Friday, Paul Marshal Curry, 58, of Salina, Kansas, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the 1994 murder of his wife, Linda Curry, whom he poisoned with nicotine. He showed no emotion as Orange County Superior Court Judge Patrick Donahue handed down the sentence. Curry called 911 on June 9, 1994, claiming he found Linda unresponsive in bed. She had been married to him for only two years. Though police suspected foul play at the time, insufficient evidence prevented charges. The day after Linda’s funeral, Curry began pursuing her life insurance policy and ultimately received $547,000. Prosecutors argued that over the course of a year, Curry slowly poisoned his 50-year-old wife with nicotine before administering a fatal dose alongside a powerful sedative. In 1993, hospital staff discovered lidocaine in Linda’s IV bag during a hospitalization for unexplained vomiting, headaches, and bloody diarrhea — a red flag that went uninvestigated at the time. The case remained dormant until 2007, when advances in forensic science narrowed the timeframe of the fatal nicotine injection. Curry was arrested in Kansas in 2010 and convicted in September 2010. During the trial, Linda’s former friend and second wife testified that Curry had urged both women to apply for life insurance shortly before they became seriously ill. When Linda’s application was denied, Curry divorced her — and her health improved dramatically, according to testimony. Curry’s defense attorney, Lisa Kopelman, contended that Linda suffered chronic gastrointestinal issues and may have self-administered nicotine as a treatment for irritable bowel syndrome. However, the jury found the prosecution’s timeline and circumstantial evidence more compelling.

No mostró ninguna emoción cuando el juez del Tribunal Superior de Orange County, Patrick Donahue, impuso la sentencia. Curry llamó al 911 el 9 de junio de 1994, afirmando que encontró a Linda sin respuesta en la cama. Había estado casado con ella solo dos años. Aunque la policía sospechaba desde el principio que había sido un crimen, no hubo suficientes pruebas para presentar cargos. Al día siguiente del funeral de Linda, Curry comenzó a reclamar la póliza de seguro de vida y finalmente recibió $547,000. Los fiscales argumentaron que, durante un año, Curry envenenó lentamente a su esposa de 50 años con nicotina antes de administrarle una dosis letal junto con un potente sedante. En 1993, el personal hospitalario descubrió lidocaína en la bolsa de IV de Linda durante una hospitalización por vómitos, dolores de cabeza y diarrea con sangre sin explicación — una señal de alerta que no se investigó en ese momento. El caso permaneció dormido hasta 2007, cuando avances en ciencia forense redujeron el intervalo de tiempo en que Curry pudo haber administrado la inyección letal de nicotina. Curry fue arrestado en Kansas en 2010 y condenado en septiembre de ese año. Durante el juicio, la segunda esposa de Curry testificó que él había instado a ambas mujeres a solicitar seguros de vida poco antes de enfermarse gravemente. article_content: Around the world, Muslims greeted the end of Ramadan with joyful cries of 'Eid Mubarak' — a celebration of community, faith, and generosity. From stadiums in Egypt to rooftops in Bangladesh, families gathered for dawn prayers, exchanged gifts, shared elaborate meals, and visited loved ones. 'Think Christmas, Thanksgiving, and New Year’s — all rolled into one,' said Sajjad Aziz of Hoboken, New Jersey. 'It’s that big for us.' Eid al-Fitr, which concludes the holy month of fasting from dawn to dusk, follows the lunar calendar. Its date depends on the sighting of the new crescent moon — so while most countries, including the U.S., celebrated on Sunday, some began festivities on Monday. 'It only takes one sighting anywhere in the country for everyone to erupt in cheers,' said Qazi Arif of Sirajgong, Bangladesh. 'It’s a divine moment — hard to put into words.' Muslims don new clothes and gather in open fields for communal prayers, often too large for mosques. Those able to do so give zakat al-fitr — a charitable donation — to ensure even the poorest can join the celebrations. 'Eid is fundamentally about community,' explained Wasim Iqbal of Karachi. 'We’re even encouraged to take a different route home from prayer so we can greet new people.' For Muslims living as minorities in places like the U.S., the celebration is quieter. 'If you have family nearby, you can recreate some of the warmth you remember back home,' said Abdallah Gamal, an Egyptian expat in St. Louis. 'But it’s not the same.' Estimates of the U.S. Muslim population vary widely — Pew Research puts it at 2.5 million; CAIR suggests up to 6 million, since the Census doesn’t track religion. In a show of solidarity, President Barack Obama and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton extended Eid greetings, with Clinton noting, 'There is more that unites people of faith than divides us.' Afghanistan’s President Hamid Karzai echoed this, urging the Taliban to embrace peace. Yet not all was harmony: Yemeni factions accused each other of violating a ceasefire meant for Eid, and Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei condemned Israel and Western powers in his sermon. Still, amid the complexities, moments of profound unity remain. 'Have you ever seen an Eid prayer?' asked Mehreen Ali of Boston. 'Row after row of Muslims prostrating together — in perfect sync. That spirit of brotherhood? It makes you believe anything is possible.'

Desde estadios en Egipto hasta techos en Bangladés, las familias se reunieron para las oraciones de la mañana, intercambiaron regalos, compartieron comidas elaboradas y visitaron a sus seres queridos. 'Piensa en Navidad, Acción de Gracias y Año Nuevo — todo combinado en uno', dijo Sajjad Aziz de Hoboken, Nueva Jersey. 'Es así de grande para nosotros.' Eid al-Fitr, que da fin al mes sagrado de ayuno desde el amanecer hasta el anochecer, sigue el calendario lunar. Su fecha depende del avistamiento de la nueva luna creciente — por lo que, mientras la mayoría de los países, incluido Estados Unidos, celebraron el domingo, algunos comenzaron las festividades el lunes. 'Solo se necesita un avistamiento en cualquier parte del país para que todos estallen en vítores', dijo Qazi Arif de Sirajgong, Bangladés. 'Es un momento divino — difícil de poner en palabras.' Los musulmanes visten ropa nueva y se reúnen en campos abiertos para oraciones comunitarias, a menudo demasiado grandes para las mezquitas. Aquellos que pueden ofrecen zakat al-fitr — una donación caritativa obligatoria — para asegurar que incluso los más necesitados puedan participar en las celebraciones. 'Eid es fundamentalmente sobre comunidad', explicó Wasim Iqbal de Karachi. 'Incluso se nos anima a tomar un camino diferente al regresar de la oración para saludar a nuevas personas.' Para los musulmanes que viven como minorías en lugares como EE.UU., la celebración es más tranquila. 'Si tienes familia cerca, puedes recrear algo del calor que recuerdas de casa', dijo Abdallah Gamal, un egipcio en St. Louis. 'Pero no es lo mismo.' Las estimaciones de la población musulmana en EE.UU. varían ampliamente: Pew Research sitúa la cifra en 2.5 millones; CAIR sugiere hasta 6 millones, ya que el censo no pregunta por afiliación religiosa. En muestra de solidaridad, el presidente Barack Obama y la secretaria de Estado Hillary Clinton extendieron saludos por Eid, con Clinton diciendo: 'Hay más que une a las personas de fe que las divide.' El presidente afgano Hamid Karzai hizo eco de esto, instando a los talibanes a abrazar la paz. Sin embargo, no todo fue armonía: facciones yemeníes se acusaron mutuamente de violar un alto el fuego declarado para conmemorar Eid, y el líder supremo iraní, el ayatolá Khamenei, condenó a Israel y a las potencias occidentales en su sermón. article_content: When Carol Roe stands at her back gate, she can see her granddaughter’s grave across the road. On August 2, 2014, 22-year-old Julieka Dhu — an Aboriginal woman from Geraldton — was arrested for an unpaid $1,000 fine. Three days later, she was dead. 'My granddaughter got killed in custody,' Ms. Roe told Daily Mail Australia. 'She’s lying over there when she should be sitting with me in my backyard.' Julieka Dhu died in police custody on August 4, 2014. An autopsy revealed broken ribs and bleeding on the lungs, but could not determine the exact cause of death. Her family still does not know why she was jailed, how she sustained her injuries, or why she was returned to the South Hedland police watch-house despite needing urgent medical care. Malcolm Dick Wilson, the man in the neighboring cell, said Dhu cried out in pain for hours while police ignored her. Her boyfriend, Dion Ruffin, recalled that when officers finally took her to hospital, they joked she was 'acting.' He said he heard one officer shout, 'Get up,' followed by a loud thud — then silence. Almost three months later, no definitive answers have been given. Carol Roe is leading a Change.org petition with nearly 53,000 signatures, demanding a timely coronial inquest and an independent body to investigate all deaths in custody — not internal police reviews. WA Premier Colin Barnett acknowledged the investigation has taken longer than it should and pledged that the coroner will uncover the full truth. WA Police have committed to submitting their internal report to the coroner by the end of October 2014. Roe and hundreds marched in Perth, Geraldton, and Port Hedland on October 23, 2014, calling for justice and a renewed Royal Commission into Aboriginal deaths in custody. Since the original 1987 inquiry, more than 400 Indigenous Australians have died in custody — a number that continues to rise, fueled by disproportionately high incarceration rates. In Western Australia, 38% of those in custody are Indigenous; among youth, it’s 64%. 'Enough is enough,' Roe said. 'Too many have died — now my granddaughter.'

article_content: (CNN) — Park Ji-sung’s return to Manchester United has been delayed after the South Korean midfielder sustained a hamstring injury during training. The English Premier League leaders had been without the 29-year-old for the past six weeks while he competed in the Asian Cup in Qatar, and he now faces up to another month on the sidelines. Park injured his hamstring on Friday, just before the Manchester derby, and will miss United’s UEFA Champions League last-16 tie against Marseille on February 23. 'It was very unfortunate — it was his last touch of the ball in training,' manager Alex Ferguson told the club’s website on Tuesday. United had been eager to welcome him back after his month-long absence at the Asian Cup. His absence is a significant blow. Park has not played for United since their 2-0 win over Sunderland on December 26. He was part of the South Korea squad that reached the semifinals of the January Asian Cup before losing to eventual champions Japan. Following the tournament, Park announced his retirement from international football, citing a persistent right-knee injury as a primary reason. In addition to the Champions League match, Park will also miss Saturday’s FA Cup fifth-round game against non-league side Crawley Town, as well as upcoming Premier League fixtures against Wigan, Chelsea, and Liverpool. He may return in time for the second leg against Marseille on March 15. On a positive note, Ecuadorian winger Antonio Valencia has resumed training after recovering from an ankle fracture sustained in a Champions League match against Scottish side Rangers in September. 'Valencia began training with the reserves on Saturday,' Ferguson said. 'He’s on his way back, and having him available for the run-in will be a real boost.' Valencia, who signed from Wigan for a reported $27 million in July 2009, was a regular starter during United’s second-place finish last season but has made only two Premier League appearances this term.

article_content: Furious residents have condemned a group of vandals who damaged a Christmas tree dedicated to teenage cancer hero Stephen Sutton. Hundreds of yellow ribbons had been tied to the tree, erected in Burntwood, Staffordshire, last weekend in memory of the late teenager. Just days after his mother, Jane Sutton, switched on the lights in front of hundreds of supporters, individuals ripped off clusters of ribbons and broke branches and lights. Organizers now fear they may be forced to install tall fences around the tree to prevent further attacks. The tree was installed to honor Stephen Sutton, who died in May 2014 after a three-year battle with colorectal cancer. Yellow ribbons became a nationwide symbol of support after Stephen raised £5 million for the Teenage Cancer Trust before his death. His inspirational bucket list — 46 things he wanted to do before dying — went viral, capturing global attention. Stephen, who was just 19 when he passed away, was posthumously awarded an MBE last month. Joanne Jarvis, a family friend who organized the ribbon tribute, said she was 'gutted' by the vandalism. 'I’ve been in tears,' she said. 'We thought it might have been the wind, but we now know the ribbons were deliberately torn off. I’m disgusted.' Jarvis spent weeks selling ribbons for charity, raising an additional £1,500 for Stephen’s cause. Residents are calling for the culprits to be punished. Keith Willis-Croft, vice chair of Burntwood Town Council, and Jane Sutton were present at the tree-lighting ceremony. Jeremy French, a 45-year-old local welder, said: 'It’s disgusting. The police must review CCTV and find these people immediately. These ribbons were bought to honor a hero.' Anne Timber, 67, added: 'You wonder about some people these days. If locals found out who did this, they’d make them pay. Stephen was a shining light.' Brian Cooper, a Burntwood Town Council officer, noted this wasn’t the first time the town’s Christmas tree had been targeted — in past years, youths had pushed it around. 'We hoped this year, dedicated to Stephen, would be different,' he said. 'But some ribbons were knocked off — we’ve reattached them. If it happens again, we’ll have no choice but to erect a two-meter fence.' Staffordshire Police confirmed they are investigating the incident. Stephen was diagnosed with colorectal cancer in September 2010. After initial remission, the cancer returned and spread to his pelvis by 2011, deemed incurable. He then created his bucket list, which included skydiving, playing drums at Wembley, writing a book, getting a tattoo, crowdsurfing, and hugging an elephant. What began as a goal to raise £10,000 snowballed into £5 million for the Teenage Cancer Trust. He met Prime Minister David Cameron and footballer Frank Lampard, both of whom praised his courage. Stephen died on May 14, 2014, at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham. Tributes poured in from David Cameron, Ed Miliband, comedian Jason Manford, and others. Cameron called him 'an inspiration,' saying, 'A very, very bright light has gone out.' Manford described him as 'better than us' — someone who, in his darkest hours, selflessly devoted his final days to helping others.

article_content: Have you heard the one about the comedian who earns more than most Premier League footballers? Publicly available financial records reveal that Britain's top comedians — men and women alike — are raking in fortunes that rival, and often surpass, those of high-profile football stars. Peter Kay tops the list, earning £32.8 million over the past two years — the equivalent of roughly £45,000 per day. According to the Sunday Mirror, the 39-year-old Bolton-born star channels his income through his companies, Goodnight Vienna and Hussein Traders. His earnings even exceed those of Premier League star Wayne Rooney, who earns £11 million annually. These extraordinary figures reflect a seismic shift in comedy: today’s top stand-ups now fill stadiums like pop icons, a far cry from the days when comedians performed in small theatres and pub backrooms. Michael McIntyre, 37, ranks second with earnings of £21 million over two years. John Bishop, 46, comes in third with £6.3 million in the same period. Jack Dee, 51, is fourth, having made £5.2 million in just one year. Russell Howard, 33, follows at fifth with £4 million over two years. The highest-earning woman on the list is Sarah Millican, 37, from the North of England, with £2 million. The lure of big money has drawn many comedians back onto the road. Kay returned to touring after a seven-year break. Bishop, who announced a two-year hiatus in May of the previous year, launched a new tour just five months later. Even veteran comedian John Cleese, 72, embarked on a two-month 'Alimony Tour' following his £12.5 million divorce settlement.

article_content: After leaving office, Tony Blair built a lucrative private career — earning up to £150,000 per speech and amassing a property portfolio worth over £25 million. But a leaked 2010 contract reveals another layer: he was paid £41,000 a month by PetroSaudi, an energy firm co-founded by Prince Turki bin Abdullah Al Saud, Saudi Arabia’s late king’s son. In exchange, Blair agreed to connect PetroSaudi with influential figures in China — politicians, industrial leaders, and corporate decision-makers — not in the Middle East. The agreement, signed through his consultancy Tony Blair Associates, also granted him a 2% cut on any successful deals he helped close. Both parties vowed to keep the arrangement secret unless they gave mutual permission to disclose it. Critics say this undermines his credibility as a volunteer Middle East peace envoy for the UN, EU, US, and Russia, especially given Saudi Arabia’s poor human rights record. Blair’s team insists the work had zero connection to his diplomatic role and was strictly about expanding business opportunities in Asia. PetroSaudi, which operates in Ghana, Indonesia, Venezuela, and Tunisia, confirmed the engagement lasted only four to five months. Meanwhile, Blair has faced past backlash for halting a UK corruption probe into arms sales to Saudi Arabia and advising authoritarian leaders like Kazakhstan’s Nursultan Nazarbayev. Though he denies being worth £100 million, his post-premiership earnings paint a picture of a global advisor operating at the highest financial tiers — and raising tough questions about transparency.

article_content: Three young women—Becky Connery, Lizzie Leeland-Cunningham, and a third person who prefers to remain anonymous—united after discovering they were all secretly dating the same man, 20-year-old Charlie Fisher. Each believed she was his only partner, unaware he had been seeing all three at once for months. The revelation came when Becky, while at Fisher’s house the night before his trip to Germany, noticed a suggestive text on his phone. Suspicious, she reached out to the sender via Twitter and learned the woman had also been seeing him. A similar discovery on Facebook led them to the third woman. Together, they pieced together a timeline suggesting Fisher had slept with each of them in rapid succession—including possibly all three within a single day. Frustrated and hurt, they decided to confront him publicly at Luton Airport as he returned from vacation. Chanting 'liar' and 'cheat,' they caught him off guard. Fisher froze, then tried to walk away with his grandmother, who had come to pick him up. The women followed, demanding answers. Though shocked, none of them regretted the confrontation. In the aftermath, the three women formed a close friendship, finding solidarity in their shared experience. Fisher, who has not responded to requests for comment, has since ended all contact and made no further attempts to reconcile.

article_content: A pensioner was found brutally murdered in her home following a suspected burglary. The body of 86-year-old widow Una Crown, who lived alone and had no children, was discovered in her bungalow on Magazine Lane, Wisbech, Cambridgeshire, shortly after 11 a.m. on Sunday. Detectives initially treated the death as unexplained, but a post-mortem examination confirmed she died from a violent assault. Detective Chief Inspector Jon Hutchinson said: 'Mrs. Crown died as a result of a brutal assault in her own home. She was last seen by family members at 11 a.m. on Friday and made a phone call to a friend at 6 p.m. on Saturday night. Officers believe she was killed sometime overnight.' Hutchinson stated the case is not linked to any other crimes in the area, but a possible motive could be a break-in. There is no evidence of sexual assault, and the property was not ransacked. 'Searches and checks are ongoing to determine if entry was forced,' he added. 'It is too early to say what the motive was. This is a close-knit community, and we are speaking with her family and neighbors. Our investigation is still at an early stage, and we are working to reconstruct the events leading to her death.' Mrs. Crown’s husband, Jack Roland Crown, died on Boxing Day 2009 after 60 years of marriage. Neighbors described her as a 'perfect neighbor' with 'a heart of gold.' One anonymous neighbor said, 'We’re so shocked this could happen. She was so vulnerable. How could anyone do this?' They noted she had been lonely since her husband’s passing. Another neighbor, Maureen Lawrence, said: 'I can’t remember exactly when I last saw her, but she seemed normal and without worry. When I heard she had died, I assumed, given her age, it was peaceful — but now learning otherwise is devastating. We haven’t noticed any crime or suspicious activity in this quiet, friendly street.' Anyone with information is urged to contact the Major Crime Unit on 101 or Crimestoppers anonymously at 0800 555 111.

article_content: David Oliver Relin, the co-author of the best-selling book Three Cups of Tea, died by suicide at age 49, a year after the book’s factual claims were widely questioned. Relin was found dead on November 14, 2012, in Corbett, Oregon, from a blunt-force head injury, according to medical examiners. No further details were released. His family stated that the married journalist and humanitarian 'suffered from depression,' and a police statement with additional information was expected that week. Relin co-wrote Three Cups of Tea with Greg Mortenson, which chronicles Mortenson’s efforts to build schools in Pakistan and Afghanistan. The book sold over four million copies after its 2006 release. In April 2011, '60 Minutes' and author Jon Krakauer exposed numerous fabrications in the book, including claims that some schools never existed, Mortenson was never lost in Korphe, and he was never kidnapped by the Taliban. Mansur Khan Mahuud, identified as one of the men alleged to have kidnapped Mortenson, clarified to '60 Minutes' that he was not a captor but a protector, calling the claim 'totally false.' Critics also accused Mortenson’s charity, the Central Asia Institute, of financial mismanagement, including diverting funds to promote the book. A lawsuit filed by readers alleging fraud was dismissed by U.S. District Judge Sam Haddon in 2011, who called the claims 'overly broad, flimsy, and speculative.' Mortenson denied intentional deception but acknowledged 'some omissions and compressions' in the narrative. He later repaid more than $1 million to the charity for personal expenses incurred during book promotion. Relin, who had a distinguished career in humanitarian journalism—winning over 40 national awards—did not publicly respond to the allegations but hired a lawyer to defend himself in the lawsuit. Book agent Elizabeth Kaplan told the New York Times the partnership between Relin and Mortenson was strained from the start. Mortenson, often unreachable due to travel, was criticized by Relin for being named co-author despite doing little writing. During a 2011 interview, Mortenson stated Relin did 'nearly all the writing' and that the book’s narrative was shaped from conflicting memories and editorial choices. Relin, born in Rochester and based in Portland, also reported extensively from East Asia and completed a new book before his death, about doctors fighting cataract blindness in the developing world. It was scheduled for spring publication. He is survived by his wife, Dawn, his mother, stepfather, and two sisters. Mortenson, 52, continues to live in Montana with his family and remains active in educational advocacy.

article_content: A mother allegedly suffering from mental illness was found dead in the basement of her home alongside her nine-year-old daughter. Ariana Rosa-Soares, 32, and her daughter Marley were discovered in the basement of their residence in Brockton, Massachusetts, on Friday morning. Police have not commented on whether the deaths constitute a murder-suicide, but a homicide investigation has been opened. Authorities emphasized there is no ongoing threat to the public. Both individuals were found deceased. Police were called to the home around 9:45 a.m. after Rosa-Soares failed to pick up Marley from a friend’s house. The family’s residence is located in a suburban area of Brockton, approximately 25 miles from Boston. Officials reported finding written material at the scene but declined to disclose its content or confirm whether it was a suicide note. Outside the home, Rosa-Soares’s father, Jose Rosa, expressed deep distress, stating he had long been concerned about her mental health and parenting abilities. He told the Boston Globe he believed his daughter was mentally unwell, though he could not confirm if she had received a formal diagnosis. He added, 'My daughter, she is not a good mother... I tried to get help to stop what happened now.' Rosa said the Massachusetts Department of Children and Families had previously been contacted for assistance. Rosa-Soares was divorced from Marley’s father and had another child, age 11, who was staying with a friend at the time of the incident. She moved to the United States from Cape Verde, an island nation off the west coast of Africa, roughly a decade ago. State police and Brockton local authorities are jointly investigating. Autopsies are expected within the next few days. According to the Boston Globe, police found written material in the basement but did not elaborate further. Friends told WCVB that Rosa-Soares had mentioned suicidal thoughts in the past, though no immediate signs of imminent danger were observed.

article_content: In the quiet village of Lathuile, near Lake Annecy in eastern France, a woman was shot and killed in a brutal home invasion. The attack occurred around 2 a.m. at the Ideal camping site, a popular destination for British tourists. Two masked men, wearing cagoules and gloves, broke in and attacked the couple who owned and operated the site. The woman was fatally shot in the chest, while her husband was struck on the head with the butt of a weapon. Though injured, he managed to flee inside and barricade himself under the stairs. After a single gunshot, he found his wife dead. The assailants escaped in a dark sedan. This tragedy comes just over a year after the 2012 murder of the British-Iraqi al-Hilli family — Saad al-Hilli, his wife Ikbal, his mother-in-law Suhaila al-Allaf, and French cyclist Sylvain Mollier — in nearby Chevaline. That case remains unsolved. One of the al-Hilli children, seven-year-old Zainab, survived after being pistol-whipped; her younger sister, Zeena, hid in the family car. Eric Maillaud, the prosecutor leading both investigations, acknowledged the proximity of the two incidents but cautioned against assuming a direct link. 'All tracks remain open,' he said. 'The circumstances differ, and the weapons appear unrelated.' He suggested possibilities ranging from a botched burglary to a personal vendetta. Zaid al-Hilli, the brother of the slain Saad al-Hilli, was arrested in the UK in June on suspicion of orchestrating the 2012 killings. He has consistently denied any involvement and remains on bail, awaiting a January court date. French and British authorities continue to investigate both cases, struggling to identify motives or perpetrators.

article_content: Thomas Langenbach, 47, a vice president at global software giant SAP, was arrested for allegedly switching barcode labels on Lego boxes at Target stores to purchase them at deep discounts, authorities say. Langenbach, who has worked at SAP since 1988 and holds a degree in computer science and business administration from Germany’s Berufsakademie Mannheim, reportedly used his technical skills to generate fake barcodes. He then replaced the original labels on high-value Lego sets—such as the $279 Millennium Falcon model—with his own, allowing him to pay as little as $49 per set. Security personnel at a Target store in Cupertino identified Langenbach on May 8 after noticing suspicious activity and placed him under surveillance. On May 9, he was caught in the act and arrested after attempting to leave the store with an unpaid-for Lego set. During a search of his multimillion-dollar home in San Carlos, police discovered hundreds of unopened Lego boxes, carefully sorted by size, color, and style. Authorities also found a bag of pre-printed counterfeit barcodes in his vehicle. Langenbach allegedly sold more than 2,000 of these discounted Lego sets on eBay under the username 'tomsbrickyard', earning approximately $30,000. He was charged with four felony counts of burglary and posted $10,000 bail the same day. While his motive remains unconfirmed, investigators suggest it may have been driven by financial gain, boredom, or compulsive behavior. SAP, which publicly provides guidelines on barcode generation, has not commented on Langenbach’s actions. He is scheduled to appear in Santa Clara County Court for arraignment.

article_content: I’ll be honest—I’m hooked on Uber. Even though the company has been embroiled in scandal after scandal—including the horrifying rape case in New Delhi, allegations of harassing journalists, running a crass ad campaign in France that offered free rides with attractive women, and even flooding Lyft with fake ride requests to sabotage them—I still use it. Last Sunday, I took an Uber to the airport in Atlanta. When I landed in New York, I groaned at the thought of waiting in a taxi line. Uber was faster, cleaner, and way easier. And that’s the real issue: in today’s world, convenience often overrides conscience. We scroll past bad news on Facebook because it’s easier than changing our habits. Boycotting big tech feels performative, even unpatriotic, in an economy built on instant gratification and widening inequality. This isn’t just about Uber. It’s about Google, which knows too much about me, and Spotify, which pays artists pennies per stream—even though I listen to it while writing this. These companies now offer services once provided by public institutions: Google is our library, Uber our bus, Spotify our radio. But unlike public transit, they’re unregulated, rarely questioned, and face almost no competition. Sarah Lacy, a sharp critic and founder of PandoDaily, put it bluntly: ‘No one gets fired. No one is held accountable. And nothing changes.’ She deleted Uber from her phone—not just for principle, but for safety. I downloaded Lyft yesterday. But here’s the uncomfortable truth: I still want the protest to be effortless. We keep saying we care—but we won’t inconvenience ourselves enough to make a real difference.

El domingo pasado tomé un Uber para ir al aeropuerto de Atlanta. Cuando llegué a Nueva York, me quejé al pensar en la fila de taxis amarillos. Uber fue más rápido, más limpio y mucho más fácil. Hacer un boicot a las grandes tecnológicas parece pretencioso, incluso antiamericano, en una economía basada en la gratificación instantánea y la creciente desigualdad. Esto no se trata solo de Uber. Es sobre Google, que sabe demasiado sobre mí, y Spotify, que paga a los artistas centavos por reproducción —aunque lo escuche mientras escribo esto. Estas empresas ahora ofrecen servicios que antes proporcionaban instituciones públicas: Google es nuestra biblioteca, Uber nuestro autobús, Spotify nuestra radio. article_content: As one of the few countries with direct contact with both Hamas and Israel, Turkey aims to broker a lasting peace. In Istanbul, Turkey, the war in Gaza has positioned the nation as a potential mediator—not only to halt Israel’s bombardment of the Palestinian enclave but also to resolve one of the world’s most intractable conflicts. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has spearheaded Turkey’s efforts, seeking to reassert its global influence by replicating Ankara’s earlier success in mediating the Ukraine-Russia grain deal. Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel and Israel’s ongoing retaliatory strikes in Gaza occurred as Ankara and Tel Aviv were rebuilding warmer ties after more than a decade of hostility. Turkey maintains relations with Hamas, making it one of the few nations with any influence over the group that has governed Gaza since 2007. Ankara has never designated Hamas as a 'terrorist organization,' prompting protests from Israel, which claims that Hamas members based in Turkey have been involved in planning attacks against Israel. 'Turkey has a strong communication channel with Hamas, which is a vital asset,' said Taha Ozhan, research director at the Ankara Institute. 'It has been cultivated over 17 years, during which Turkey was the only country to invite Hamas into its capital.' 'In times of crisis, these channels are indispensable,' added Ozhan, a former chair of the Turkish parliament’s foreign affairs committee. Turkish officials—led by Erdogan and Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan—are leveraging this access to position Ankara as central to resolving the current Gaza conflict. Their immediate priorities include delivering humanitarian aid to civilians in Gaza and securing the release of approximately 200 hostages taken by Hamas. Speaking in Beirut on Tuesday, Fidan said, 'A variety of countries have requested Turkey’s assistance in freeing their citizens.' We have begun discussions with the political wing of Hamas,' he added. 'We are exerting significant effort to ensure the release of children and foreign nationals.' There is widespread public support in Turkey for the Palestinian cause, with thousands attending pro-Palestine demonstrations in recent days. Turkey maintained diplomatic relations with Israel for much of Israel’s history, until tensions escalated in 2010, when Israeli forces killed nine Turkish citizens aboard the Mavi Marmara—a ship attempting to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza. A tenth died years later after remaining in a coma. Relations were restored in 2016, only to deteriorate again in 2018, following Israel’s passage of the Nation-State Law, which declared Israel the 'nation-state of the Jewish people,' and the U.S. decision to relocate its embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. That same year, Israel killed dozens of protesters during the Great March of Return in Gaza. These events have cemented Erdogan’s popularity among Palestinians. 'Erdogan remains lionized in Gaza, the West Bank, and across much of the Arab world due to his consistent, forceful criticism of Israel’s policies toward Palestinians,' said Wolfango Piccoli, co-president of the political risk advisory firm Teneo. This admiration endured despite Turkey’s shift last year toward regional reconciliation—with Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and even Israel. Fidan has met with regional leaders and held calls with U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken and Hamas chief Ismail Haniyeh. Ankara, Fidan said, seeks to 'open the door to a permanent and comprehensive peace' grounded in a two-state solution and offered to serve as a guarantor. 'We do not believe lasting solutions can emerge from outdated methods,' he said during a joint press conference with Lebanon’s foreign minister. 'We hope upcoming talks will introduce new approaches.' Ozhan believes Turkey may be uniquely positioned to propose a political framework that enables serious discussions on the future of the Palestinian people. 'Unless we address this fundamental question, all outcomes will remain temporary—or arbitrary,' he said. Ferhat Pirincci, a professor of international relations at Bursa Uludag University, noted, 'From the outset, Turkey has advocated that frozen conflicts—especially those like this—can be resolved peacefully, allowing for sustainable peace.' Yet, experts warn that Turkey’s mediation could fail without meaningful engagement from both sides. 'Without confronting the reality of occupation and the plight of the Palestinian people, there is no real space for progress—only empty rhetoric,' Ozhan cautioned. 'It depends on whether Israel—and the backing it receives from Washington and Europe—is genuinely committed to mediation.' Warning of a potential regional ripple effect, he added: 'The prudent path is to rebuild a political framework and use this crisis as leverage to establish lasting diplomacy. But that depends on Israel—and on certain Western capitals.'

Ferhat Pirincci, profesor de relaciones internacionales en la Universidad Bursa Uludag, señaló: 'Desde el principio, Turquía ha abogado por que los conflictos congelados—especialmente aquellos como este—pueden resolverse pacíficamente, permitiendo una paz sostenible.' article_content: New Look has been named the favorite high street fashion brand among British women, overtaking Zara for the first time. This result comes from a six-month survey of 10,000 women conducted by dressipi.com for its annual Fashion Brands Index (FBI). In the study covering June to December 2013, 24% of respondents selected New Look as their top choice. Zara, which led in the previous 12-month period, fell to second place with 23%, reflecting a 10% decline in favorability compared to its rating in the year ending December 2012. H&M and Topshop tied for third with 21% each, both experiencing a slight 1% dip from the prior six-month period. Next ranked fifth with 17%, followed by River Island at 14%. Dorothy Perkins, Primark, and Oasis tied for seventh with 12% each, while Mango came in tenth with 10%. New Look’s rise has been fueled by strong seasonal collections, savvy celebrity partnerships — including with Kelly Brook — and widespread appeal among public figures such as Princess Beatrice, Zara Phillips, Lucy Watson, and members of the TOWIE cast. A dressipi spokesperson noted that New Look excels at translating runway trends into wearable, affordable pieces that suit multiple body types and ages. While price plays a role, the brand’s real edge lies in balancing trend, basics, versatility, and standout design. Founded in 1969 in Taunton, Somerset, New Look now operates more than 1,000 stores worldwide. Its 2013 breakthrough followed successful spring and summer lines, solidifying its status as a dominant force in UK fashion.
