article_content: President José Mujica has criticized six former Guantanamo Bay detainees for appearing 'middle class' and lacking a work ethic, after they declined job offers following their relocation to Uruguay three months ago. The men — detained in 2002 as suspected militants with alleged ties to al-Qaeda but never charged — were cleared for release in 2009 but remained imprisoned due to an inability to return home and a lack of other countries willing to accept them. Uruguay stepped in, offering housing, Spanish language instruction, cultural orientation, and assistance finding employment through local labor unions. Despite these efforts, the men have turned down multiple job offers, including positions in construction, prompting Mujica to visit the homes of five of the six men personally. During a radio broadcast, Mujica expressed disappointment, stating the detainees did not resemble the 'gritty, hardworking peasants' who built modern Uruguay. 'Through their hands, features, and family histories, it seems to me they’re middle class,' he said. The men, however, describe their new reality as 'swapping one prison for another.' One, Abu Wa'el Dhiab, a Syrian who cannot return due to ongoing conflict, told reporters he needs more than shelter — he needs family reunification, stable housing, employment, and income to rebuild his life. Dhiab, who lost the ability to walk after 13 years in Guantanamo and later began using crutches following prolonged hunger strikes, has become a vocal advocate for better support. Human rights lawyer Cori Crider of Reprieve UK confirmed Dhiab’s medical condition and emphasized the profound psychological toll of prolonged detention. Senator Ope Pasquet of Uruguay’s Colorado Party defended the men, noting the severe trauma they endured and calling immediate work demands 'premature.' While Uruguay has provided a safe haven, critics argue the government lacks a comprehensive reintegration strategy — leaving the men in limbo, neither free nor fully supported.

article_content: By David Martosko, U.S. Political Editor. The Mississippi Tea Party battle isn’t over yet. An attorney for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Chris McDaniel told reporters on Monday that his campaign expects to uncover enough evidence of voter fraud in the June 24 primary runoff to trigger a new election. That would mark the third head-to-head contest between McDaniel and six-term Senator Thad Cochran, a 76-year-old moderate Republican whose support for immigration reform and other center-left policies made him a prime target for the Tea Party movement. McDaniel’s campaign counsel, Mitch Tyner, said Monday he ‘would be surprised if we don’t find’ enough fraudulent votes to invalidate the June 24 results. He claimed the campaign has already identified ‘thousands’ of irregularities. Last week, an initial review of ballots flagged at least 4,900 potential irregularities. A GOP runoff win for Sen. Thad Cochran could be short-lived if McDaniel proves that more ineligible votes were cast than his margin of victory. Cochran and McDaniel first faced off on June 10. McDaniel won the most votes, but neither secured at least 50%, triggering a runoff two weeks later. Complaints of fraud surfaced even before polls closed, primarily centered on a seven-figure super PAC supporting Cochran that ran ads encouraging Democrats in predominantly Black counties to ‘cross over’ and vote in the Republican primary. While such crossover voting is legal under Mississippi law — provided voters haven’t participated in their own party’s primary — McDaniel’s team argues that many of these votes were cast illegally. Tyner stated Monday that state law mandates ‘automatically a new election’ if the number of ineligible voters exceeds the margin of victory — approximately 6,700 votes. An election adviser in Hattiesburg told MailOnline that McDaniel doesn’t need to prove 6,700 fraudulent votes were cast *for* Cochran — any 6,700 ineligible votes would suffice. ‘Most of them,’ he said, ‘are going to be absentee ballots. It’s too easy to scam, and nobody ever checks unless the margin is this close or the result this unexpected.’ On Monday, as the Mississippi Republican Party faced a 5:00 p.m. deadline to certify the runoff results, McDaniel’s team fanned out across the state to work with county clerks examining absentee ballot applications. Tyner said in a brief press conference that until Monday, campaign representatives hadn’t been allowed inside courthouses to inspect ballot boxes — including absentee records. ‘That is what we’re going after today,’ he said. Cochran’s campaign appears unfazed. His spokesman, Jordan Russell, said in a statement: ‘We have representatives at all 82 courthouses today to monitor the review of ballot boxes and have been pleased with the results.’ Russell told The Associated Press that Cochran’s team found only one crossover vote out of more than 2,000 cast in Perry County; three out of 4,000 in Pontotoc County; five out of 2,000 in Leake County; and seven out of more than 11,000 in Lauderdale County. But radio ads and flyers targeting Black communities — particularly in Hinds County, home to over 169,000 Black residents — included messages attempting to tie McDaniel to the Ku Klux Klan to motivate Democratic turnout. 'All Citizens for Mississippi,' a political committee that did not legally exist prior to launching these materials, is among the shadowy groups behind the negative advertising. Haley Barbour, former Mississippi governor and former Republican National Committee chairman, founded the super PAC responsible for the ads. 'It is imperative that an ineligible voter not be excluded from this,' Tyner said Monday. 'Because when I vote and there’s an ineligible voter that also votes, he dilutes my vote. He dilutes your vote.' McDaniel can challenge the result even after certification, but he may also seek a court injunction to block the party from finalizing its numbers. More likely, he’ll file a formal challenge with the state GOP, followed by litigation after a 10-day review period. If Cochran’s victory is overturned, the correct remedy, Tyner said, is a new election. The eventual winner will face former Democratic Congressman Travis Childers in a general election expected to deliver a Republican senator in this deeply red state. Nationally, the Republican Party is on the brink of reclaiming control of the U.S. Senate — a milestone not seen since 2007.

article_content: A 58-year-old Chinese national, Jia M. Tian, was arrested Monday at the Washington National Cathedral and held without bond on Tuesday. She was carrying a soda can filled with green paint when apprehended. Prosecutors and court documents link Tian to at least four other acts of vandalism, including damage to the Lincoln Memorial, a statue of Joseph Henry outside the Smithsonian, and a statue of Martin Luther in Thomas Circle. In a church near Thomas Circle, Tian allegedly splashed a pipe organ with a mixture of white paint, feces, and urine. Tian, who is in the U.S. on an expired visa, has no fixed address but told officers she lives in Los Angeles. Police say she speaks little English and may have underlying mental health issues. Her motives remain unclear. At the National Cathedral, green paint was found splattered on organs and decorative woodwork in two chapels — Bethlehem Chapel and Children’s Chapel. The paint was still wet when discovered, indicating recent activity. Tian was wearing green-painted clothing and shoes, and a multicolored sock on her right arm. A matching sock was later found in a cathedral bathroom atop a can of green paint. Three bags found at the scene contained additional cans of green paint. Cleanup efforts at the cathedral are estimated to cost $15,000. Restoration at the Lincoln Memorial is ongoing and may take several days. The National Park Service confirmed that the paint on the Lincoln Memorial was deliberately applied, though symbols on the statue remain undeciphered. The memorial was briefly closed but reopened the same day. Authorities plan to send paint samples from the cathedral to the FBI for forensic analysis. Surveillance footage from Bethlehem Chapel is under review. Tian appeared in D.C. Superior Court Tuesday alongside a Mandarin interpreter. A judge ordered her to reside in a halfway house and wear an ankle monitor.

article_content: On September 21, 2013, Elaine Dang, a 26-year-old American expat working in Nairobi, survived a horrific assault at the Westgate Shopping Mall — one of the deadliest terrorist attacks in Kenya’s history. While dining with colleagues that afternoon, she was caught in a barrage of gunfire from at least 15 heavily armed militants linked to Al-Shabaab. She suffered multiple gunshot wounds to her chest, arm, and leg, requiring emergency surgery. Two of her close friends did not survive. From her hospital bed, Dang turned to social media to share her story. A photo she posted showed her smiling faintly beside friends in a Nairobi ward, captioned: 'Proof that I am OK — hanging out with some of my best friends in Nairobi.' Her messages overflowed with gratitude: 'Thank you for all the love and support — in Kenya and overseas. Terrorism knows no religion.' Her father, Steven Dang, spoke to U.S. media from their home in San Diego, confirming her injuries and expressing both anguish and relief. 'I cried. I was terrified. But now… she’s going to be okay,' he said. He described how a piece of metal pierced her chest during the chaos, a detail echoed in medical reports. Meanwhile, Kenyan journalist Mohammed Ali of KTN shared rare CCTV footage showing two armed men wandering the mall’s corridors — not in uniform, but dressed casually, carrying rifles. The images drew comparisons to the 2008 Mumbai attacks, underscoring the global nature of such threats. Kenya’s military leadership, including General Julius Karangi, stated the attackers were not locals but part of a transnational network. Intelligence suggested foreign nationals were involved, though specific nationalities were not officially disclosed. Despite the trauma, Dang’s public voice remained focused on compassion. She urged people to remember the hundreds still injured or trapped, writing: 'In moments of true chaos — the impossible can happen.' Her words became a quiet anthem of resilience amid horror.

article_content: At Emory University, a team of historians is breathing life back into the forgotten identities of millions of Africans forcibly taken across the Atlantic. Their tool? Names—real, original names recorded in 19th-century court documents from places like Havana and Freetown. These weren’t just labels; they carried meaning. A name might reveal whether someone was born on a Tuesday, was a twin, or belonged to the Yoruba or Akan people. For decades, these names sat buried in dusty archives, stripped of context. Now, researchers are asking descendants—anyone with African roots—to step forward if they recognize a familiar name in their family stories. Among the thousands of names documented? Two men named Obama, recorded on slave ship registries decades before a U.S. president bore the same name. While there’s no evidence connecting them, the coincidence has sparked powerful reflection. As Professor David Eltis explains, African names are linguistic fingerprints: precise, culturally rich, and capable of pointing to specific villages or regions. The project, African-Origins, doesn’t just collect names—it revives voices. One researcher from Ghana discovered his own family name, and those of his siblings and children, in the records. ‘We’ve been taught to think of slavery as faceless,’ he says. ‘But these names? They’re faces. They’re ancestors.’ The database now includes audio recordings of how these names might have sounded in their original languages, helping people hear what was lost. The ships that carried them—the Xerxes, the Midas—were horrors on water: overcrowded, deadly, armed. Of the 429 souls aboard the Xerxes in 1828, 26 died before reaching port. On the Midas, 162 never made it. Those who survived were sometimes returned to Africa—but rarely home. Many ended up in Liberia or stayed free in Caribbean ports. Others vanished into new enslavement. Though the records rarely track what happened after liberation, this project gives something invaluable: a starting point. For families searching for roots, for scholars piecing together history, and for anyone who wants to remember: these were not numbers. They were people—with names, with origins, with stories waiting to be told.

article_content: In a high-stakes diplomatic push, US Secretary of State John Kerry arrived in Geneva to join talks aimed at reaching a temporary agreement with Iran over its nuclear program. Joining foreign ministers from China, Russia, the UK, France, and Germany, Kerry’s presence signals urgency as negotiators race to lock down a six-month deal. The proposal would freeze key parts of Iran’s nuclear activities in return for modest sanctions relief — buying time for more complex negotiations later. At the heart of the discussions is Iran’s long-standing demand to enrich uranium — a process that can be used for civilian energy or weapons. While Iran insists its program is purely peaceful, Western powers remain deeply skeptical, citing past concealment efforts. Yet behind closed doors, Iranian officials hinted that they might accept a deal without an explicit written guarantee of their enrichment rights — a notable shift from public statements by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei. Meanwhile, France has pushed back against rushing into an agreement, warning that any deal must be robust and verifiable. Germany acknowledged progress but stressed that major hurdles remain. Russia sounded cautiously hopeful, calling the talks 'very close' to a breakthrough, while China labeled them 'the final moment' in the process. Other concerns include Iran’s undeclared plutonium reactor in Arak and how to ease sanctions without eroding international leverage. Domestically, both sides face pressure: Iranian hardliners fear Rouhani’s government is conceding too much, while US lawmakers argue the West is giving up too little. Despite public toughness, Iranian negotiators in Geneva suggested much of the rhetoric is aimed at domestic audiences — and that room for compromise still exists.

article_content: Nearly a year after the FDA granted approval, Belviq—a prescription weight-loss medication—is now available to eligible patients starting Tuesday. The drug, approved in June 2012, faced a delayed rollout due to additional review by the Drug Enforcement Administration. Belviq is intended for adults with a body mass index of 30 or higher, or those with a BMI of 27 or above who also have weight-related conditions like hypertension or Type 2 diabetes. The FDA emphasizes that Belviq should be used in combination with a reduced-calorie diet and regular exercise, not as a standalone treatment. Its active ingredient, lorcaserin hydrochloride, activates serotonin receptors in the brain to promote earlier feelings of fullness and reduce food intake. Clinical trials showed modest but meaningful results: patients on Belviq lost an average of 13 pounds, while those on Qsymia lost about 23 pounds. Among non-diabetic users, 47% lost at least 5% of their body weight—nearly double the 23% seen in the placebo group. For diabetic patients, 38% achieved that level of weight loss compared to 16% on placebo. Safety monitoring remains critical: the FDA requires Arena Pharmaceuticals to conduct six post-marketing studies, including a long-term cardiovascular trial. Common side effects include headache, dizziness, and fatigue. Diabetic patients may also experience low blood sugar or pain. Eisai Inc., the drug’s marketer, has noted rare cases of heart valve problems in users of similar medications, though a direct link to Belviq has not been established. The official labeling cautions: 'It is not known if Belviq changes your risk of heart attack, stroke, or death from these conditions.'

article_content: China's Commerce Minister Wang Wentao told Micron Technology's President and CEO, Sanjay Mehrotra, during a meeting on November 1, that Beijing welcomes the US semiconductor company to deepen its presence in the Chinese market—signaling a notable improvement in US-China relations. According to a brief statement released by the Ministry of Commerce on Friday, Wang emphasized that China is committed to optimizing the business environment for foreign investors and providing support services to international enterprises. 'We welcome Micron Technology to continue taking root in the Chinese market and achieving better development, provided it complies with Chinese laws and regulations,' Wang said. This outreach comes just months after China’s cyberspace regulator barred key infrastructure operators from purchasing Micron’s memory chips, a move widely interpreted as retaliation for US restrictions on advanced chip technology exports to China. The timing aligns with broader diplomatic shifts: the G7 recently agreed to pursue 'de-risking, not decoupling' from China, while the US continues pressuring allies to limit semiconductor equipment sales to Beijing. The meeting also reflects growing momentum toward a high-level dialogue between US President Joe Biden and Chinese President Xi Jinping, planned for late November at the APEC summit in San Francisco.

Según un breve comunicado publicado por el Ministerio de Comercio el viernes, Wang enfatizó que China se compromete a optimizar el entorno empresarial para los inversores extranjeros y brindar apoyo a las empresas internacionales. article_content: Built as a dream home for property developer Neil Ryan, High Oak—a luxurious five-bedroom mansion in Hockley, Essex—is now on the market for £4 million. The 14,000-square-foot property sits on 1.4 acres of landscaped gardens and features an opulent reception hall with twin staircases, a first-floor sun terrace with a swimming pool, a soundproof home cinema, a wine cellar, a gym, and eight reception rooms. Ryan purchased the land in April 2006 for £900,000, demolished the existing house, and completed construction two years later. The master suite and four additional bedroom suites each include dressing rooms and en-suite bathrooms. The first-floor terrace, designed as a private pool area, includes a dedicated kitchen and bathroom to avoid disrupting the main living spaces. Interior finishes include hand-painted solid walnut kitchen units, top-of-the-range appliances, underfloor heating throughout, and air conditioning in the bedrooms, cinema, and gym. The home’s cinema boasts upholstered padded walls, fitted seating, surround sound, and a large projector screen linked to DVD and Sky. Neil Ryan, founder of Neil Ryan Bespoke Homes, specializes in designing custom homes for wealthy clients, primarily based in London. John Seward of Strutt & Parker in Chelmsford, the listing agent, noted significant interest and multiple viewings already scheduled. He added: 'This is the home Ryan built for himself—many rooms have never been lived in. It’s that new.' Chartered Surveyor Robert Burns from Tillett Burns & Hughes commented: 'Properties like this exist in their own market segment. Buyers don’t rely on mortgages—they travel across the UK for such rare offerings. These homes can even elevate property values in surrounding neighborhoods.'

article_content: Cancer scientists are borrowing techniques from astronomy to detect faint biomarkers in aggressive tumors. Methods originally developed to identify distant galaxies are now being adapted to spot subtle patterns in stained tumor samples — potentially replacing the traditional practice of manually examining cells under a microscope. Traditionally, aggressive tumors are identified by staining tissue to highlight specific proteins. Astronomers use a technique called a 'standard ruler' to measure distances between celestial objects. Researchers have repurposed this concept into an automated system designed to detect and quantify protein levels in cancer samples. In tests involving over 2,000 breast cancer patient samples, scientists measured levels of three key proteins. They compared the results generated by human analysts with those produced by the automated system. The computer-based method matched the accuracy of manual analysis — while being significantly faster. Dr. Raza Ali, lead scientist at Cancer Research UK’s Cambridge Institute, explained: 'We’ve leveraged the natural overlap between how astronomers analyze deep-space images and how pathologists assess tumor staining. The results have exceeded our expectations — our automated tool performs with precision comparable to manual scoring, after only minor tweaks to the algorithm.' The team plans to expand the study internationally, analyzing samples from more than 20,000 breast cancer patients to further refine the method. Co-author Professor Carlos Caldas noted: 'Modern diagnostics are uncovering critical genes and proteins that predict treatment outcomes. But validating these markers requires analyzing thousands of samples — a task now made feasible by automation. We can process up to 4,000 images daily, accelerating the path from discovery to clinic.' Dr. Nicholas Walton from Cambridge’s Institute of Astronomy added: 'It’s rewarding to see software built to search for habitable exoplanets now helping improve outcomes for cancer patients right here on Earth.' The research, conducted in partnership with Cambridge University astronomers, has been published in the British Journal of Cancer.

En pruebas que involucraron más de 2.000 muestras de pacientes con cáncer de mama, los científicos midieron los niveles de tres proteínas clave. article_content: Robin van Persie kept his scoring streak alive ahead of the World Cup, netting the only goal in the Netherlands’ 1-0 victory over Ghana in Rotterdam. Just five minutes in, Sneijder spotted Van Persie making a smart run and slid a low pass across the box — the striker tapped it in before the goalkeeper could react. The Dutch controlled the ball from start to finish, but their attack lacked the final precision needed to kill the game early. Arjen Robben, in particular, missed several golden opportunities: one from barely three yards out after a perfect cross from Blind, another after a clever through-ball from Janmaat, and a third when his angled shot was saved at close range. Despite dominating territory, the Dutch struggled to break Ghana’s low block with fluidity, often resorting to isolated efforts rather than cohesive build-up. Memphis Depay came on late but couldn’t add to the tally. Meanwhile, Ghana rarely threatened, failing to register a single serious chance. Coach Louis van Gaal, who recently trimmed his squad from 29 to 23 players, looked pleased with the win but clearly wants more cutting edge before facing Spain, Chile, and Australia. With this match likely being his last in charge of the Oranje before heading to Manchester United, Van Gaal’s experimental 5-3-2 formation — morphing into 3-5-2 or 3-4-3 when fullbacks pushed forward — gave fans a glimpse of what might come in the Premier League. But for now, the real story remains Van Persie: five goals in just over three hours since returning from injury, proving he’s still the man to rely on when it matters most.

article_content: Acapulco, Mexico (CNN) — Six suspects arrested and accused of sexually assaulting a group of Spanish tourists in the Mexican resort city of Acapulco have confessed, a top official said Wednesday. Attorney General Jesús Murillo Karam declared the case 'resolved,' though one suspect remains at large. 'There are already six arrests; all have fully confessed to the details of what happened, and we only need to apprehend one more person identified in this investigation,' he said. 'The case is solved.' The allegations, which emerged last week, drew widespread attention across Mexico and globally. Authorities said hooded gunmen stormed a beach bungalow in the Pacific port of Acapulco, raping six women and binding a group of men with cell phone cables and bikini straps. Investigators have not yet determined whether the suspects — including one who is 16 and therefore a minor — are affiliated with a gang, Murillo Karam said. They also have not confirmed claims by local authorities that the suspects may have encountered the victims days before the attack. One suspect was arrested Tuesday, and five others were taken into custody Wednesday morning following 'a very serious investigation,' he added. All six have confessed. Murillo Karam clarified that earlier detentions announced over the weekend were unrelated to this case. The high-profile incident in the popular resort city has once again highlighted persistent security challenges in Guerrero state, where violence has surged even as homicide rates decline in other parts of Mexico. The case has revived public discourse on issues President Enrique Peña Nieto had sought to sideline since taking office in December. CNNMexico.com, journalist Salomon Kaufman, Laura Reyes, and CNN’s Jessica King, Alexander Hunter, Catherine E. Shoichet, and Michael Martinez contributed to this report.

article_content: Long ago, Mars wasn't the dry, frozen desert we see today—it was a world where water moved beneath its surface, possibly creating conditions favorable for life. New data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express mission have uncovered 175 distinct rock formations in the ancient highlands of Tyrrhena Terra, all showing clear signs of having been altered by water—deep underground. These minerals weren’t shaped by rain or rivers on the surface. Instead, asteroid impacts punched through the crust, digging up rocks that had been slowly transformed by groundwater hundreds of millions of years ago. The altered minerals, including clays and other silicates, suggest water circulated kilometers below the surface, at temperatures as high as 300°C, for an extended period—possibly over a billion years. This means Mars didn’t just have fleeting bursts of water; it sustained a complex, hidden hydrological system long before most of its craters even formed. Even areas far from craters show traces of these minerals, hinting that the entire ancient crust was chemically reshaped by water, not just spots near impact zones. Scientists believe this deep, long-lived water flow could have created environments capable of supporting microbial life. The discovery paints a picture of an active, dynamic Mars—one where water didn’t just flow on the surface, but simmered quietly beneath, shaping the planet’s hidden geology.

article_content: A guard was freed Thursday night after being held hostage by inmates at a South Carolina maximum-security prison for nearly five hours, authorities said. The incident occurred at Lee Correctional Institute in Bishopville — a facility where another guard was held hostage in June. Bishopville is approximately 55 miles west of Columbia, the state capital. The incident began just before 5 p.m. ET in the prison’s Chesterville dormitory, according to Clark Newsom, a public information officer for the South Carolina Department of Corrections. The guard, whose identity was not disclosed, was rescued just before 10 p.m. by a large team of officers, Newsom said. He sustained cuts to his head and arm but was able to walk out of the facility after being freed. As a precaution, the guard was airlifted to a hospital, Newsom added. The inmates involved surrendered, and the incident is under investigation, according to CNN affiliate WLTX. In June, a different guard at the same facility — which houses about 1,200 inmates — was held hostage for several hours before being rescued. Lee Correctional Institute is a Level 3, or maximum-security, prison 'designed primarily to house violent offenders with longer sentences and inmates who exhibit behavioral problems,' according to the Corrections Department’s website. 'Yes, we are examining security issues — we always do,' Newsom said. 'This is a maximum-security facility where the most dangerous individuals are held. Unfortunately, these kinds of incidents can still occur despite our efforts.' Previous incident: South Carolina prison guard rescued in June.

article_content: WASHINGTON (CNN) — The U.S. Navy has deployed the guided-missile destroyer USS Cole and other vessels to the eastern Mediterranean Sea off the coast of Lebanon, Pentagon officials said Thursday. A file image of the USS Cole, which the U.S. Navy moved to the Mediterranean near Lebanon, was released alongside the announcement. The deployment comes amid a political stalemate over Lebanon’s presidency, though the Navy declined to confirm any direct connection. 'It’s a group of ships that will operate in the vicinity for a while—and, as ships in our Navy do, their presence is important,' said Adm. Mike Mullen, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, on Thursday. 'It isn’t meant to send any stronger signal than that,' he added. 'But it does signal that we’re engaged and will remain in the vicinity, which is a very important part of the world.' The USS Cole was severely damaged in a 2000 al-Qaeda bombing during a port call in Yemen, killing 17 sailors. It returned to active service in 2002. The destroyer and two support ships are positioned near Lebanon but beyond visual range of the coastline, according to Pentagon officials. Another six vessels, led by the amphibious assault ship USS Nassau, are en route from waters near Italy to join them. Mullen refused to link the deployment to Lebanon’s 15th postponement of its parliamentary vote for a new president, which occurred earlier this week. However, he acknowledged the vote as 'important,' noting Washington’s anticipation of its occurrence. A Bush administration official, speaking anonymously, told CNN the move sends a message to neighboring Syria: 'The U.S. is concerned about the situation in Lebanon, and we want to see it resolved.' 'We are sending a clear message for the need for stability,' the official said. Lebanon’s pro-Western parliamentary majority and pro-Syrian opposition have clashed for power over the past three years. The country has remained without a president since November 2007, when Emile Lahoud’s term ended and lawmakers failed to agree on a successor. Although all major factions support naming Army Chief Gen. Michel Suleiman as president, disputes over cabinet power-sharing have stalled the vote. Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri’s office announced Tuesday that the next session has been rescheduled for March 11, citing the Arab League’s need for more time to mediate the deadlock. Since the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri—whose supporters blamed Syria—the nation has endured violent political turmoil. Public outrage following Hariri’s death ultimately forced Syrian troops to withdraw from Lebanon, ending nearly three decades of military presence since the 1970s. CNN correspondent Zain Verjee contributed to this report.

Se publicó una imagen archivada del USS Cole, que la Armada de EE.UU. movió al Mediterráneo cerca del Líbano, junto con el anuncio. El despliegue ocurre en medio de un estancamiento político sobre la presidencia del Líbano, aunque la Armada se negó a confirmar una conexión directa. 'Es un grupo de barcos que operará en la zona durante un tiempo, y como hacen los barcos de nuestra Armada, su presencia es importante', dijo el almirante Mike Mullen, presidente de los Jefes de Estado Mayor, el jueves. 'No pretende enviar ninguna señal más fuerte que esa', agregó. 'Pero sí señala que estamos comprometidos y permaneceremos en la zona, lo cual es una región muy importante del mundo.' El USS Cole sufrió graves daños en un ataque de al-Qaeda en 2000 durante una escala en Yemen, matando a 17 marineros. Regresó al servicio activo en 2002. El destructor y dos embarcaciones de apoyo están posicionados cerca del Líbano pero fuera del rango visual de la costa, según funcionarios del Pentágono. Otros seis buques, liderados por el buque de asalto anfibio USS Nassau, están en ruta desde aguas cercanas a Italia para unirse a ellos. Mullen se negó a vincular el despliegue con el decimoquinto aplazamiento de la votación parlamentaria del Líbano para elegir un nuevo presidente, que tuvo lugar a principios de esta semana. Sin embargo, reconoció que la votación es 'importante' y señaló la expectativa de Washington por su realización. Un funcionario de la administración Bush, hablando en anonimato, le dijo a CNN que la medida envía un mensaje a Siria, su vecina: 'EE.UU. está preocupado por la situación en el Líbano, y queremos verla resuelta'. 'Estamos enviando un mensaje claro sobre la necesidad de estabilidad', dijo el funcionario. La mayoría parlamentaria prooccidental del Líbano y la oposición prosiria han luchado por el poder durante los últimos tres años. El país ha permanecido sin presidente desde noviembre de 2007, cuando finalizó el mandato de Emile Lahoud y los legisladores no lograron acordar un sucesor. Aunque todas las facciones principales apoyan nombrar al jefe del ejército, el general Michel Suleiman, como presidente, las disputas sobre la distribución del poder en un futuro gabinete han retrasado la votación. La oficina del presidente del Parlamento, Nabih Berri, anunció el martes que la próxima sesión se reprogramó para el 11 de marzo, citando la necesidad de más tiempo por parte de la Liga Árabe para mediar en el impasse. Desde el asesinato en 2005 del ex primer ministro Rafik Hariri —cuyos seguidores culpaban a Siria—, la nación ha sufrido una agitación política violenta. La indignación pública tras su muerte obligó finalmente a las tropas sirias a retirarse del Líbano, poniendo fin a casi tres décadas de presencia militar desde los años setenta. article_content: A distraught father cradles the body of his six-year-old son, Chien Hao, who was buried alive while building sandcastles on an unsecured construction site in Xiamen, Fujian Province, southeastern China. Chien died after a dump truck reversed and unloaded a load of sand onto him as he played with his eight-year-old sister and a friend. The two girls managed to escape in time and raised the alarm. Builders, firefighters, and Chien’s parents rushed to dig him out with their bare hands to avoid causing further injury with tools. By the time Chien was freed, he was unconscious and unresponsive. Paramedics were unable to revive him. Local police confirmed the construction site had not been properly secured. The children had entered the area unsupervised. Survivors said they did not notice the truck reversing toward them with a fresh load of sand. Chien’s parents are demanding legal action against the construction company for failing to secure the site and against the truck driver for not checking his surroundings before dumping. Police spokesman Ho Hung said: 'We are investigating following a complaint by the parents. The boy was buried for about an hour before recovery. Rescue teams used only their hands to prevent additional trauma. Sadly, after being crushed under tons of sand and deprived of oxygen, he had already died.'

article_content: Passenger Nora Low lost luggage worth over £2,000 on a British Airways flight from Amsterdam to Lake Tahoe, California, following a computer glitch that disrupted baggage handling at London Heathrow Airport. The incident was part of a larger system failure affecting approximately 40,000 bags during the same period. Low, who was traveling to attend her brother’s birthday, described the experience as devastating. Her suitcase contained clothing valued at around $4,000 (£2,000), along with essential medication. When she tried contacting British Airways, customer service lines were unreachable, and voicemail systems were full. Frustrated and desperate for answers, Low turned to Twitter. There, she discovered dozens of other passengers facing identical issues. Together, they formed an online support network, sharing updates and amplifying their collective grievances. It wasn’t until ABC News reached out to Low and began covering the story that British Airways responded. After public exposure, the airline contacted her directly, offering to process her claim. Low received a £1,945 compensation check and an additional £300 goodwill payment—totaling £2,245. However, she reported the actual value of her lost items as £2,385, leaving a £140 shortfall. In a social media post, she wrote: 'I wish I lived in London so I could go look for my luggage myself. I know it’s still there.' Other passengers echoed her anguish, describing the ordeal as 'mental torture.' In a statement to MailOnline Travel, British Airways apologized, acknowledging the glitch caused bags to go missing when tags fell off. They confirmed ongoing efforts to locate remaining luggage and assured customers they would be compensated fairly. Low concluded: 'Travel nightmare; lesson learned the hard way. I’m never going to check a bag ever again.'

article_content: Twelve-year-old Zachary Reyna is fighting for his life after contracting Naegleria fowleri, a rare and deadly amoeba that attacks the brain. The Florida Department of Health has issued a caution to swimmers, noting that elevated water temperatures and low water levels create conditions where the organism thrives. Zachary was kneeboarding in a shallow freshwater ditch near his home on August 3 when he was likely exposed. The next day, he slept through almost the entire day — an unusual sign for such an active seventh-grader. His mother rushed him to the hospital, where he underwent emergency brain surgery and was diagnosed with primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM). He is now receiving care in the ICU at Miami Children's Hospital. The CDC has coordinated with his medical team and provided an experimental drug called Impavido — the same treatment that helped 12-year-old Kali Hardig survive a similar infection in Arkansas. Kali is one of only three people in the past half-century to recover from PAM. Her family reports remarkable progress: she can now sit up independently, write on a whiteboard, stand with help, and even play catch with therapists. Her doctor, Dr. Vikki Stefans, credits Kali’s strong support system and says her recovery is no longer in doubt — only the extent of her full recovery remains to be seen. While infections from Naegleria fowleri are exceedingly rare — only 32 cases were recorded in the U.S. between 2001 and 2010 — they are almost always fatal. The amoeba enters through the nasal passages during activities in warm freshwater, not through drinking water. It is most commonly found in the southeastern United States, particularly in stagnant or slow-moving bodies of water. In Kali’s case, health officials believe Willow Springs Water Park in Little Rock was the likely source; after two suspected cases tied to the same location, the park voluntarily closed, even though its water is regularly tested and treated. Early signs of infection include headache, fever, nausea, and neck stiffness, followed by confusion, seizures, and hallucinations. Symptoms typically appear within a week and progress rapidly, often leading to death within days. To reduce risk, the CDC advises avoiding freshwater activities during hot weather, using nose clips, not disturbing sediment in shallow waters, and using only distilled or boiled water for sinus rinses like neti pots.

article_content: On Wednesday, I met with S. Ganbaatar, a respected independent member of Mongolia’s parliament. He walked straight over to a framed document hanging in my office — a relic from 1996 known as the 'Contract with the Mongolian Voter.' It was signed by dozens of candidates who pledged to uphold a shared platform of private property rights, press freedom, and foreign investment if elected. That promise resonated deeply with voters: in a landslide with 91% turnout, they ousted the Communist Party, which had ruled since 1921. Ganbaatar, who himself entered parliament in 2012, called this moment a turning point — saying those words 'gave us our freedom.' It wasn’t accidental that Ganbaatar visited just before the 20th anniversary of the U.S. 'Contract with America.' Back in 1994, over 350 American candidates stood on the Capitol steps and pledged to deliver ten specific reforms if they won control of the House. That bold move — not just a list of policies, but a binding promise — helped Republicans take the House for the first time in four decades. What made it powerful wasn’t the details, but the principle: elected officials owe the people honesty, follow-through, and accountability. If they failed, voters could kick them out. And they didn’t fail. In their first 100 days, they delivered balanced budgets, welfare reform, and major tax cuts. The U.S. Contract didn’t just change Congress — it reshaped American politics. For the first time since 1928, a Republican majority was re-elected. Since then, they’ve held the House for 16 of the last 20 years. But more than its political impact, the real legacy is how it inspired others — like Mongolia — to try something radical: make politicians answerable before they even take office. In places where authoritarianism once ruled, this idea — that power belongs to the people, not the party — became a lifeline. Ganbaatar’s visit reminded me: democracy isn’t a one-time victory. It’s a daily promise. And it only survives when leaders never forget who put them there.

article_content: David Moyes suffered his seventh Premier League defeat of the season as Manchester United fell 3-1 to Chelsea at Stamford Bridge — a result that all but ended their title hopes. In response, betting firm Paddy Power installed a lifelike waxwork of Sir Alex Ferguson outside Old Trafford, posed in his signature 'Fergie Time' stance inside a glass box labeled 'In Case of Emergency: Break Glass.' The stunt, widely interpreted as a satirical nod to United’s collapse, has sparked intense fan reaction. Ferguson, who managed United for 26.5 years and won 13 Premier League titles, retired in 2013. His return — even in wax — symbolizes the stark contrast between past glory and current struggles. A Paddy Power spokesperson quipped that Jose Mourinho had 'hammered the final nail into the coffin' of United’s season, adding that the glass box might be shattered faster than a Wayne Rooney promise of loyalty. Despite being 14 points behind leaders Arsenal and sitting seventh in the table, Moyes refused to concede defeat. 'That’s your word, not mine,' he said of the term 'crisis.' 'We won’t throw in the towel until we can’t get there.' Defender Phil Jones echoed this optimism, insisting United are 'not a million miles away' from the league’s elite, citing a strong first-half performance as proof. But he admitted costly defensive errors and missed opportunities cost them the match. United now turn their focus to the Capital One Cup semi-final second leg against Sunderland, trailing 2-1. They will be without central defender Nemanja Vidic, serving a three-match ban after receiving a red card against Chelsea. Jones emphasized the need for unity: 'We need to stick together if we’re going to turn it around.' The emotional weight of Ferguson’s presence — even as a statue — underscores the deep yearning among fans for the stability and success of a bygone era. For now, the question remains: Is this an emergency... or just the beginning of a longer rebuild?

article_content: Two experienced hikers, Connie Yang and Suzanne Turell, safely descended Colorado’s Longs Peak on their own after being stranded for two days by a severe ice storm. The National Park Service had been preparing a rescue mission when the women managed to make their way down without injury. The climbers, both 32 and 33 years old and based in York, Maine, sent urgent text messages to Yang’s sister as conditions worsened. One message read: 'We need help. At top of Longs Peak. 13,400 feet. Their texts prompted the creation of a Tumblr page to update friends and family. Trapped inside their tent amid whiteout conditions, they remained calm despite raging floods below that blocked access roads and prevented rescue teams from reaching them. Yang and Turell are experienced mountaineers who spent several weeks hiking the Pacific Crest Trail last year and work for NEMO Equipment Inc., a New Hampshire-based outdoor gear manufacturer. They had begun a week-long backpacking trip in Rocky Mountain National Park and were stranded approximately 800 feet below the 14,259-foot summit.

article_content: Buenos Aires, Argentina — Just four days after being elected president, right-wing populist Javier Milei is already facing fierce resistance from Argentina’s labor unions and social organizations. They are vowing protests if he follows through on his pledge to drastically shrink the state and privatize key industries. Milei, who famously campaigned with a chainsaw to symbolize his intent to cut public spending, argues that radical reforms are essential to revive Argentina’s stagnant economy and tame its staggering 140% annual inflation. The day after his decisive 56%-to-44% electoral victory, he told a radio interviewer: 'Everything that can be in the hands of the private sector will be.' His targets include state-owned media, oil and gas firms, and potentially water distribution and rail services — even ending all public infrastructure projects. Labor leaders say these proposals directly threaten workers’ livelihoods and national development. Héctor Dear, secretary general of the powerful General Confederation of Labor (CGT), stated after a meeting with union heads: 'Our vision for the country centers on production and job creation — but Milei’s talk of cuts and privatizations moves in the opposite direction.' The strongest reaction came from Pablo Biró, head of the Airline Pilots Association, who declared: 'He will have to literally kill us' to privatize Aerolineas Argentinas. While many union leaders are adopting a cautious wait-and-see stance — acknowledging that Argentines voted for Milei — others have already drawn a line in the sand. Daniel Catalano, head of the State Workers’ Association, said during a protest march alongside the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo: 'We expect absolutely nothing from Javier Milei.' The weekly demonstration by the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo — originally focused on human rights abuses during Argentina’s 1976–1983 military dictatorship — took on a new political dimension as activists joined to symbolically oppose Milei’s agenda. Leftist social groups convened separately to organize a broader 'plan for struggle against austerity,' signaling planned street protests. Meanwhile, analysts warn of inevitable unrest. Nicolás Saldías of the Economist Intelligence Unit noted: 'A lot of labor unions are highly mobilized — this is a high-stakes situation for them.' Milei has openly acknowledged the coming hardship, warning of 'six tough months' ahead but insisting they will lay the foundation for recovery. 'There is no money,' he repeated. 'The law will be applied, and I will not let myself be extorted.' Argentina’s tradition of powerful, street-based labor movements — combined with a historical reluctance by authorities to use force against protesters due to past violence — means Milei’s reforms could trigger one of the nation’s most intense social conflicts in decades.

article_content: The capture of Osama bin Laden wasn’t the result of a dramatic military strike alone—it was the culmination of nearly a decade of relentless work by a quiet but fiercely determined CIA analyst. Known internally as 'Jen,' she was the one who insisted the key to finding the world’s most wanted man lay not in broad surveillance, but in tracking a single, elusive courier: Abu Ahmed al-Kuwaiti. While others doubted, she stood firm, betting her career on a hunch that eventually led U.S. forces to a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan. Her intensity didn’t win her friends. Colleagues described her as sharp-tongued, obsessive, and unwilling to compromise—even when it meant clashing with senior officials. She reportedly once told Navy SEALs she’d rather bomb the compound than risk lives in a raid, a stance that stunned many. Yet, when the mission succeeded, she was among the few awarded the CIA’s highest honor, the Distinguished Intelligence Medal. Still, she felt betrayed: while dozens received lesser accolades, she believed her singular contribution deserved far more. The film Zero Dark Thirty, directed by Kathryn Bigelow and written by Mark Boal, brought her story to the public as 'Maya,' portrayed by Jessica Chastain. The character mirrors Jen’s demeanor: emotionally reserved, morally ambiguous, and utterly focused. Unlike the glamorous, emotionally intuitive Carrie Mathison of Homeland, Maya doesn’t cry over coffee or seek validation—she stares down bureaucracy with cold precision. But behind the cinematic version lies a deeper human cost. After the raid, Jen broke down—crying silently as Bin Laden’s body was uncovered. She had spent half her adult life chasing one man, and when she finally saw him, it wasn’t triumph she felt—it was exhaustion, grief, and the weight of what she’d endured. Even after the mission, she was reassigned, passed over for promotion, and left feeling invisible despite having changed history. Her legacy isn’t just about catching a terrorist—it’s about what happens when a woman refuses to play nice in a system built for men. She didn’t need to be likable to be right. And maybe, that’s why they struggled to reward her.

article_content: (CNN) — Rocio Moreno says it took more than five years to leave her abusive husband. Throughout their marriage, she says she endured unwanted sexual advances. Whenever she challenged his control over where she went or who she spent time with, he responded with verbal and physical abuse. She finally decided enough was enough the day he hit her in front of their son. 'When he hit me, I realized he could kill me,' she said. 'I decided: no more violence. I didn’t want my son to see him treat me that way.' She left him two years ago and moved into her own home. She kept the ordeal largely private until she found the courage to share her story through the Monument Quilt — a collection of hundreds of survivor narratives currently touring the country this summer. Her words, written in Spanish, are etched onto a 4-foot red square that sits alongside others in a 16-foot display. When fully assembled, the 250 individual squares form a 100-foot multicolored quilt. 'You told me you loved me,' she writes, 'but now I know and understand that I was raped. I was your wife, not your property.' The Monument Quilt is the brainchild of Baltimore-based activist group Force: Upsetting Rape Culture. The project is making 13 stops across 12 states, displaying portions of the quilt in public spaces and expanding through community quilt-making workshops. According to Rebecca Nagle, co-founder of Force, the project evolved from discussions about creating a permanent national monument to survivors of rape — modeled after war memorials — based on research showing how public memorials aid trauma recovery. Quilting has deep roots in social justice movements, most notably through the AIDS Memorial Quilt, which began touring the U.S. in 1988 to honor those lost to the disease. Nagle hopes the Monument Quilt will similarly reduce stigma around sexual violence by encouraging public conversation and shifting blame away from survivors. 'When we remove the stigma from rape and can speak openly without blaming victims, we take one step closer to ending this epidemic,' she said. The quilt transforms parks, sports fields, and town squares into sacred spaces for reflection and grief, according to Karen Taylor, a Baltimore social worker who volunteers with Force. 'It creates a community holding space, rather than placing the entire burden of trauma on the shoulders of each individual survivor,' Taylor said. 'It can be solidifying, reassuring, even uplifting. You’re not alone anymore.' Healing also comes from the act of creating the quilt squares, many of which are crafted in workshops held weeks before the quilt arrives in a community. Force partners with local organizations focused on prevention and public safety to host these workshops. In White River, South Dakota, the White Buffalo Calf Women Society hosted two weeks of quilting sessions ahead of the quilt’s display at a local high school. Quilting is a traditional art form among the Sioux people, making the project culturally resonant for the community. 'It gave them a voice without forcing them into the spotlight — and that, in itself, was incredibly powerful,' said Summer Lunderman, the society’s education outreach coordinator. 'Standing in solidarity with other women in our community and across the U.S. was deeply empowering — it showed them they weren’t alone.' Creating her own square brought up painful memories for Lunderman, who was sexually abused as a child. Her square reads: 'Lakota Women Are Sacred.' 'It created a safe space for me that I truly needed,' she said. Witnessing the quilt inspired Baltimore activist Melanie Keller to confront her own history of rape. Though she works with the anti-street harassment group Hollaback! BMore, Keller had never publicly identified as a survivor. She noted that media coverage of sexual violence often centers on stranger danger, date rape, or the experiences of white, middle-class college students. Seeing the diversity of voices in the quilt motivated her, as a biracial woman, to contribute her own square. 'What I love about this project is the narrative of control reclaimed by survivors,' she said. 'It honors the diversity of experiences — because we’re the ones telling our stories, in our own words.' For Moreno, making her square was cathartic. She hopes sharing her story will inspire others to break free from the despair she once knew. 'Reading these words tells you: yes, there is an opportunity to break the cycle of violence,' she said. 'It doesn’t have to be like this.'

article_content: Low vitamin D levels could make childbirth more painful, scientists have warned in a new study. A team in the U.S. discovered that women were more likely to opt for an epidural to manage labor pain if they were vitamin D deficient. The researchers measured the vitamin D levels of 93 pregnant women before delivery. All participants had requested an epidural for pain relief during labor. The team then assessed the amount of pain medication each woman required. They compared the dosage of pain medication used by women with higher vitamin D levels to those with lower levels. Findings presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Anesthesiologists in New Orleans revealed that women with lower vitamin D levels required significantly more pain medication than those with higher levels. Dr. Andrew Geller, an anesthesiologist at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles and senior author of the study, said: 'Women often experience lower-than-normal levels of vitamin D during pregnancy. We found that patients with low levels experienced increased pain during childbirth.' While vitamin D deficiency has long been associated with depression and chronic pain, this is the first study to specifically link it to heightened labor pain. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists notes that vitamin D deficiency is common during pregnancy, particularly among high-risk groups including vegetarians, women with limited sun exposure, and ethnic minorities. Vitamin D is primarily obtained through fortified milk and juice, fish oils, and dietary supplements. The study authors estimate that 41% of pregnant women in the U.S. are deficient in vitamin D, with another 41% having insufficient levels. Dr. Geller added: 'Given these findings, preventing and treating low vitamin D levels in pregnant women could significantly reduce labor pain for millions of women annually. This topic warrants further research to improve the labor experience for women everywhere.'

article_content: Tens of thousands of birds are being killed each year over California by intense solar radiation from the world’s largest solar thermal plant, the Ivanpah Solar Power Facility in the Mojave Desert. Workers at the plant refer to the smoke trails left by burning birds as 'streamers.' Federal wildlife investigators observed birds igniting mid-flight and falling, estimating an average of one 'streamer' every two minutes. Estimates of annual bird deaths vary widely: BrightSource Energy reports about 1,000, while experts from the Center for Biological Diversity suggest up to 28,000. Federal officials cite approximately 30,000. The $2.2 billion plant, operational since February, uses over 300,000 mirrors—each the size of a garage door—to focus sunlight onto three 40-story boiler towers, generating steam to power turbines that supply electricity to 140,000 homes. Wildlife officials warn the plant may act as a 'mega-trap': its bright light attracts insects, which draw in insect-eating birds that then fly into the concentrated solar flux and perish. Plant operators dispute that all 'streamers' are caused by birds, noting that insects and airborne debris can also ignite under the intense heat. The California Energy Commission is now reviewing BrightSource Energy’s proposal to build an even larger facility—a 75-story tower near Joshua Tree National Park—on a major bird migration corridor rich in protected species like golden eagles and peregrine falcons. Experts say the proposed site could be nearly four times as lethal to birds as Ivanpah. While no proven method yet exists to prevent these deaths, BrightSource is researching deterrents such as sound, light, or other technologies. To offset projected bird mortality, BrightSource has offered $1.8 million for programs like spaying and neutering domestic cats—an initiative grounded in a government study showing cats kill over 1.4 billion birds annually—but critics argue this does not address the immediate threat to desert birds. Environmental advocates, including the Audubon Society, urge regulators to halt new permits until a full year of bird mortality data—including migration seasons—is collected and analyzed. Renewable energy experts stress that while all energy sources carry trade-offs, diversity in technology is essential—and no single solution should be dismissed outright.

article_content: The Mumbai Police arrested Lalit Patil, the mastermind behind a multi-crore mephedrone racket dismantled by the Pimpri-Chinchwad Police in 2020, in Chennai on Tuesday night—days after he escaped from Pune’s Sassoon General Hospital. A senior IPS officer from Mumbai Police confirmed to The Indian Express that Patil was apprehended by a Sakinaka Police team in Chennai and is now being brought to Mumbai. Patil, who had been in judicial custody since 2020, escaped on October 2 from Sassoon Hospital while receiving treatment for hernia and tuberculosis. Earlier this month, Sakinaka Police, under the supervision of Joint Commissioner of Police (Law and Order) Satyanarayan Chaudhary and DCP Zone X Datta Nalawade, raided a factory in the MIDC area of Nashik and seized large quantities of drugs. The factory is believed to be owned by Bhushan Patil, Lalit’s brother. According to police sources, a monitored phone call led to Lalit’s arrest. After the Nashik drug bust, authorities withheld the identity of a key suspect arrested alongside other racket members. When Lalit noticed that this individual’s name did not appear in media reports, he assumed the person had evaded capture. Lalit then called the suspect from an unknown number—while the suspect was still in police custody. Police allowed the suspect to speak with Lalit without revealing his detained status. Using the call metadata, Sakinaka Police traced the number and arrested Lalit in Chennai. Further investigations revealed that after fleeing Pune, Lalit traveled by rented car through Gujarat and Karnataka before settling in Chennai, frequently changing locations to evade detection. After his initial arrest by Pimpri-Chinchwad Police in December 2020, Lalit was lodged in Yerwada Central Prison. In June 2023, he was transferred to Sassoon Hospital for medical treatment. On October 2, the day before his scheduled hernia surgery, Lalit escaped. Pune Police later found that he had been using hospital staff to smuggle contraband: Rauf Rahim Shaikh, a canteen worker, delivered drugs to aide Subhash Janaki Mandal, who was arrested near the hospital on September 30 with over 1.71 kg of mephedrone valued at ₹2.14 crore. During a search of Lalit’s hospital ward, police seized two iPhones, each worth ₹1.1 lakh. An FIR was filed against Patil, Mandal, and Shaikh at Bund Garden Police Station under the NDPS Act. Bhushan Patil and Abhishek Balkawade were also named as accused in the September 30 drug seizure case. On October 10, the Pune City Police Crime Branch, in coordination with Uttar Pradesh Police’s Special Task Force (STF), arrested both men near the Nepal border. Post-arrest investigations confirmed that Lalit, Bhushan, and Abhishek jointly operated the mephedrone manufacturing unit in Nashik—the same facility later raided by Mumbai Police.

Patil, quien estuvo bajo custodia judicial desde 2020, escapó el 2 de octubre del Hospital Sassoon mientras recibía tratamiento para una hernia y tuberculosis. A principios de este mes, la Policía de Sakinaka, bajo la supervisión del Comisionado Adjunto de Policía (Ley y Orden) Satyanarayan Chaudhary y el DCP Zona X Datta Nalawade, allanó una fábrica en el área MIDC de Nashik y decomisó grandes cantidades de drogas. Se cree que la fábrica pertenece a Bhushan Patil, hermano de Lalit. Según fuentes policiales, una llamada telefónica monitoreada llevó al arresto de Lalit. Tras el allanamiento en Nashik, las autoridades ocultaron la identidad de un sospechoso clave arrestado junto con otros miembros de la red. Cuando Lalit notó que el nombre de este individuo no aparecía en los informes mediáticos, asumió que había logrado evadir a la policía. Lalit luego llamó a este sospechoso desde un número desconocido — mientras el sospechoso aún estaba bajo custodia policial. La policía permitió que el sospechoso hablara con Lalit sin revelar su estado detenido. Usando los metadatos de la llamada, un equipo de la Policía de Sakinaka rastreó el número y arrestó a Lalit en Chennai. Investigaciones adicionales revelaron que, tras huir de Pune, Lalit viajó en un automóvil alquilado a través de Gujarat y Karnataka antes de establecerse en Chennai, cambiando frecuentemente de ubicación para evitar ser detectado. Tras su arresto inicial por la Policía de Pimpri-Chinchwad en diciembre de 2020, Lalit fue encarcelado en la Prisión Central de Yerwada. En junio de 2023, fue transferido al Hospital Sassoon para tratamiento médico. El 2 de octubre, el día antes de su cirugía programada para la hernia, Lalit escapó. La Policía de Pune descubrió más tarde que había estado utilizando al personal del hospital para contrabandear drogas: Rauf Rahim Shaikh, un trabajador de la cafetería, entregaba drogas al cómplice Subhash Janaki Mandal, quien fue arrestado cerca del hospital el 30 de septiembre con más de 1,71 kg de mefedrona valorados en ₹2,14 crores. Durante un registro en la habitación del hospital de Lalit, la policía decomisó dos iPhones, cada uno valorado en ₹1,1 lakh. Se presentó una denuncia penal contra Patil, Mandal y Shaikh en la comisaría de Bund Garden bajo la Ley NDPS. Bhushan Patil y Abhishek Balkawade también fueron nombrados como acusados en el caso de decomiso del 30 de septiembre. El 10 de octubre, la Rama de Crímenes de la Policía de Ciudad de Pune, en coordinación con la Fuerza Especial (STF) de la Policía de Uttar Pradesh, arrestó a ambos cerca de la frontera con Nepal. Las investigaciones posteriores a su arresto confirmaron que Lalit, Bhushan y Abhishek operaban conjuntamente la unidad de fabricación de mefedrona en Nashik, la misma instalación que luego fue allanada por la Policía de Mumbai.

article_content: Loca, a charming pug with a rare neurological condition, has captured the hearts of millions online. With over six million views on YouTube and nearly 10,000 likes on Facebook, her videos have turned her family’s home in Belfast into a viral sensation. Loca has ataxia — a harmless neurological disorder that affects coordination, causing her to lean, stumble, and occasionally roll over. But she doesn’t let it slow her down. Her owner, Mal Orr, 55, began filming her quirky movements after noticing her unique ‘goose-step’ gait. ‘I thought it was funny,’ he says. ‘I never imagined so many people would love it.’ The videos — including fan favorites like ‘Can We Have a Rabbit?’ and ‘Babysitting Ain’t Easy’ — showcase Loca’s adventures alongside her siblings Alfie, Lucy, and Layla. The family even takes all four dogs on rides together using a specially adapted motorcycle. Mal writes and performs all the songs himself, adding a personal, playful touch. He says the response from viewers has been overwhelmingly positive: ‘People with disabilities — and parents of children with disabilities — tell us these videos make them feel seen.’ While a small number of critics have accused the family of mocking Loca, Mal and his wife Alena, 45, emphasize their intent: ‘We’re not making fun of her. We’re showing that having a disability doesn’t mean you can’t live joyfully.’ Looking ahead, the family is developing a reality series featuring ‘Loca Cam’ — a tiny camera mounted on her back to capture the world from her perspective. They’re also creating holiday-themed clips targeting audiences in the U.S. and Canada, hoping to spark friendly competition for views during Independence Day and Canada Day.

article_content: In 2012, Susan Nicholson, then 52, admitted in court to letting children reside in a home so neglected it was described as hazardous. Officers responding to the property in Gateshead found floors covered in dog waste, countertops piled with trash and spoiled food, mold growing on walls, and cockroaches crawling through rooms. Dirty laundry lay scattered, and in one bedroom, dog excrement was found on the floor. Nicholson, who lived in Bensham, had been previously advised in 2009 to improve the living conditions — advice she failed to follow. She pleaded guilty to three charges of causing unnecessary suffering and three counts of child neglect under the Children and Young Persons Act 1933. Her defense acknowledged she accepted responsibility early in the process. Despite struggling with health issues, she was given a 12-month community order, including mandatory supervision, and ordered to pay £40 in court fees. The prosecution noted that the conditions had worsened gradually over several months.

article_content: On the day Rafael Nadal turned 26, two of his biggest rivals on the clay courts of Roland Garros were fighting for survival — and both made it through. Novak Djokovic, the world’s top-ranked player, clawed back from two sets down to defeat Italy’s Andreas Seppi 4–6, 6–7(5–7), 6–3, 7–5, 6–3 in a nearly five-hour marathon on Court Philippe Chatrier. Despite playing poorly in the opening sets, Djokovic credited his victory to sheer grit. 'Nothing worked today,' he admitted, 'but I never stopped believing.' This marks his 12th straight Grand Slam quarterfinal appearance. Meanwhile, on Court Suzanne Lenglen, Roger Federer, 30, held off a spirited challenge from 21-year-old Belgian David Goffin, a lucky loser who had entered the main draw only after Gael Monfils withdrew injured. Goffin, who once hung Federer’s photos on his bedroom walls, pushed the Swiss legend hard, winning the first set 7–5 before Federer rallied to win 5–7, 7–5, 6–2, 6–4. Federer praised Goffin’s instincts and touch, calling the match 'interesting' and the young player 'full of potential.' For Goffin, ranked 109th at the start of the tournament, it was the breakthrough of a lifetime — becoming the first lucky loser to reach the last 16 of a Slam since 1995. Nadal’s next opponent is Argentina’s 13th seed, Juan Monaco, who will face the Spaniard in what’s expected to be his toughest test yet at this year’s French Open. Elsewhere, quarterfinal matchups remain undecided as Jo-Wilfried Tsonga leads Stanislas Wawrinka 6–4, 7–6(8–6), 3–6, 3–6, 4–2, and Juan Martin del Potro holds a 7–6(8–6), 1–6, 6–3 advantage over Tomas Berdych — both matches paused due to fading light. Goffin’s rise has already lifted his ranking to 68th, and while he didn’t advance further, his run has become one of the most inspiring stories of the tournament.

article_content: Manchester City delivered a stunning 6-0 thrashing of Tottenham Hotspur at the Etihad Stadium, turning heads across the Premier League. Sergio Aguero, who scored twice, earned high praise from manager Manuel Pellegrini, who placed him among the world’s three best players—alongside Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. Jesus Navas opened the floodgates in just 14 seconds after Tottenham goalkeeper Hugo Lloris mishandled the opening kick-off, giving Navas a clear chance to slot home from a tight angle. Lloris compounded his troubles minutes later, failing to clear a shot from Aguero, allowing Álvaro Negredo to tap in the rebound. An own goal from Sandro made it 3-0 before Aguero added his second with a clinical finish from Navas’s low cross. Yaya Touré provided the assist for Aguero’s fourth goal early in the second half, and Negredo and Navas sealed the victory with two more strikes. The win propelled City to fourth in the league and underscored their dominance at home: six consecutive Premier League victories, 26 goals scored, and no defeats. Tottenham, who had conceded just six goals in their first 11 matches, were completely overrun. Manager Andre Villas-Boas offered no excuses: 'Everything went wrong for us.' In other action, Manchester United’s bid to enter the top four ended in heartbreak after a 2-2 draw with Cardiff City. Wayne Rooney put United ahead twice, but Frazier Campbell equalized with a brilliant long-range strike, and Kim Bo-kyung struck deep into stoppage time with a powerful header to deny United all three points. Meanwhile, in Serie A, Juventus reclaimed the top spot with a 2-0 away win over Livorno. Fernando Llorente opened the scoring with a thunderous volley, then set up Carlos Tevez for the second goal in the 75th minute. With Roma two points behind, Juve now lead the table heading into Matchday 12.

article_content: Rain poured over waterlogged Los Angeles on Thursday, prompting Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa to order more than 300 residents to evacuate due to imminent mudslide risks. 'We continue to urge those living in affected areas to listen to our first responders — police, firefighters, and emergency teams — who are working tirelessly to protect your safety,' the mayor said at a press briefing. By Thursday morning, over 500 residents across Los Angeles County had heeded evacuation advisories, according to Capt. Sam Padilla of the Los Angeles County Fire Department. The latest storm is part of a persistent weather pattern that began Monday, dumping more than 12 inches of rain in some coastal areas, per the National Weather Service. Flash flood watches remain active across Southern California, central Arizona, and southern Utah. Villaraigosa warned Thursday night that while the most intense phase of the storms may have passed, dangerous thunderstorms forming offshore could still bring lightning, hail, and even water spouts. Four swift-water rescue teams and two urban search-and-rescue units were on standby, with more ready if needed. Three swift-water rescues occurred Wednesday alone. No relief is expected until the weekend, raising fears of further mudslides in hillside communities stripped of vegetation by the 2009 wildfires. Rainfall totals of 1 to 4 inches are forecast across coastal zones, with isolated pockets possibly receiving up to 7 additional inches. In Pacifica, south of San Francisco, a massive mudslide left an apartment building precariously balanced on a cliff overlooking the Pacific. All four units were evacuated, and engineers warned the structure could collapse into the ocean at any moment — limiting media access to brief windows. One Southern California resident voiced frustration to KABC-TV: 'You’re asking us to stay away for five days? That’s a huge inconvenience. I’m not driving around — I’m staying put.' Despite his reservations, officials stressed evacuation orders are non-negotiable for safety. On Friday, U.S. geologists, sanitation crews, and street maintenance teams will assess damaged areas to determine when residents can safely return. Meanwhile, heavy snow closed key mountain passes — Interstate 15 at Cajon Pass and the Grapevine section of Interstate 5 — as the California Highway Patrol reported. Snowfall totals exceeded 73 inches in the San Gabriel Mountains and surpassed 35 inches in parts of Arizona. Forecasters say more snow is expected across the Sierra Nevada, southeastern Utah, southwestern Colorado, and southeastern Arizona.

article_content: Somewhere, Cristiano Ronaldo will be watching the World Cup final. He was officially the best player in the world this year — but if his great rival writes his name all over football’s greatest stage on Sunday night, who will remember that? Ronaldo went home two weeks ago. He couldn’t carry a weak Portugal team through the group stage. Whether he’ll return to such a stage remains uncertain. Lionel Messi, however, has led Argentina to Rio de Janeiro through sheer willpower. This isn’t a great Argentine side — far from it — but Messi has dragged them to the final, where they’ll face Germany, a team that has punished opponents’ mistakes with ruthless precision throughout the tournament. Germany are favorites to win, but don’t count out Messi seizing the moment to claim the final as his own. Messi has scored four goals in the tournament. His last-minute winner against Iran in Argentina’s second match is one of the standout moments of this World Cup. Equally vital was his run and pass that set up Ángel Di María for the decisive goal against Switzerland in a match Argentina barely survived. That’s what truly great players do — they make the difference when it matters most. According to his father, Messi has been physically drained as the tournament has worn on. 'I spoke with him and he said he felt like his legs weighed 100 kilos,' Jorge Messi told a Brazilian newspaper. Gary Lineker and others believe Messi hasn’t been at his best in recent weeks. But Messi doesn’t need to dominate every minute to influence the game. He chooses his moments — like the inch-perfect pass to Di María against Belgium, when he was largely quiet for long stretches. Germany may try to neutralize him by shifting Philipp Lahm from full-back into midfield or relying on Bastian Schweinsteiger’s tactical awareness. But fixating on Messi risks leaving others open — as Holland discovered when Ezequiel Lavezzi thrived in the semi-final. If Di María recovers from injury, Germany’s fullbacks will face another serious threat. Sergio Agüero, who has been quiet so far, could also be a wildcard — his timing is impeccable. Germany, meanwhile, have scored 17 goals across eight different players — a sign of true team strength. Argentina have only four scorers. Messi has brought his nation here, and millions have crossed borders just to witness him potentially etch his name into history. But Germany are in better form. They’ve had a more rested buildup — unlike Argentina, who played 120 minutes against Holland. Germany, on the other hand, coasted after a blistering 45 minutes against Brazil. It’s tempting to call this a battle between one man and a machine — but that undersells Joachim Löw’s side. They’re disciplined, intelligent, and lethal. Still, if Messi delivers on Sunday, he won’t just win a trophy — he’ll become legend.

article_content: A powerful YouTube video by World Animal Protection is urging tourists to reconsider booking wild animal experiences — like elephant rides — during their holidays. Many travelers are unaware of the hidden suffering behind these attractions. To expose the truth, the organization created a fake advertisement for a fictional tour company called 'Authentic Elephant Rides.' In the video, an actress portrays a staff member who proudly describes how elephants are forcibly tamed for tourist rides. 'Elephants won’t naturally allow people to ride them,' she says. 'So, to break their spirit and deliver that 'special experience,' they’re subjected to torture from a very young age.' This brutal process, known as 'phajaan' or 'the crush,' involves separating calves from their mothers, confining them in tiny enclosures chained by the leg, beating them with clubs and sharp bullhooks, and depriving them of food and sleep for days. The video concludes with chilling footage of a visibly distressed elephant, shackled to a tree, wearing a saddle and chair, desperately trying to escape. As part of its 'Before They Book' campaign, World Animal Protection has also launched an online guide to help travelers choose ethical, animal-friendly holidays. While the video focuses on elephants, the broader campaign also highlights abuses faced by tigers and other wild animals in tourism.

article_content: Abu Qatada, the radical Islamist cleric once labeled Osama bin Laden’s right-hand man in Europe, was rearrested on March 8, 2013, after authorities alleged he violated strict bail conditions. The arrest followed a 12-hour raid on his £450,000 home in North West London by the Metropolitan Police’s Counter Terrorism Command. A senior judge, Mr Justice Irwin, revoked Qatada’s bail during an emergency hearing, citing strong prima facie evidence that he had allowed mobile phones and digital storage devices—such as memory sticks—to be used inside his residence, in breach of 25 stringent conditions. He was immediately taken to high-security Belmarsh Prison. Qatada, who was granted asylum in the UK in 1994, has spent nearly a decade fighting deportation to Jordan, where he was convicted in absentia of terrorism-related offenses. However, UK courts have blocked his removal, ruling that evidence used in Jordanian trials may have been obtained through torture. The Home Office welcomed the bail revocation, calling it a necessary step given the seriousness of the alleged breaches. Officials confirmed that searches at four properties yielded no hazardous materials, and no other arrests were made. Under his bail terms, Qatada is confined to his home for 22 hours daily, barred from using mobile phones or the internet, prohibited from attending mosques or meeting unvetted visitors, and forbidden from publishing statements or leading prayers outside his immediate family. Despite being released on bail in February 2012, Qatada has received over £500,000 in public legal aid during his protracted legal battle. His case remains politically sensitive, particularly for Home Secretary Theresa May, who announced the government’s intent to pursue his deportation during a recent Conservative Party speech. A further hearing before the Special Immigration Appeals Commission (SIAC) is scheduled for March 21, where both sides will present additional evidence. Meanwhile, the UK government plans to challenge the court’s refusal to allow deportation before the Court of Appeal on Monday.
